## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{100}{20}{20}{100}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why can an accurate detection still be too late to guide a robot?_

A camera can recognize an obstacle correctly and still report where it stood before the robot moved. Exposure, readout, transport, and inference all take time, the machine keeps moving through every millisecond of it, and a shifted mount or a misread clock then places the obstacle somewhere it never stood. None of these errors lowers a detection score. The worst of them, a frame stamped with the wrong time, narrows the estimate's uncertainty around the wrong position, so the machine grows more confident as it grows more wrong. A machine that treats a recognized object as a current position spends its stopping clearance on errors nobody measured. Perception serves a moving machine only when each observation states when it was captured, where it was measured from, and how far it can be trusted, because at the causal boundary a stale or misplaced observation becomes motion that cannot be taken back, and the permission path can refuse only evidence whose age and limits it can check.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Select sensing modalities by the physical quantity, coverage, and failure limits required for a spatial decision
- Diagnose exposure, rolling-shutter, and calibration errors before measurements enter a geometric estimate
- Calculate capture-to-dispatch age and account for continued aging through downstream consumption without double charging delay
- Evaluate whether qualified spatial error and stopping margins fit the available clearance
- Set a clearance inset from residuals measured against ground truth and a clock-conversion bound from measured synchronization error, rather than from a reported covariance or a datasheet
- Distinguish qualified metric evidence from learned depth estimates and semantic confidence
- Design an observation record whose timing, calibration, error qualification, and health checks support downstream use

:::
## Choosing Evidence for a Spatial Decision {#sec-perception-photons-to-claims}

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-opening-age
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ OPENING SCENE: OBSERVATION AGE AT THE RACK END
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The opening paragraph of @sec-perception-photons-to-claims;
# │          also the temporal-batching paragraph and the clock-sync pitfall.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show how far the warehouse mobile manipulator travels while its
# │          navigation camera's observation of a person ages.
# │ Show:    t_age 51.6 ms; 77.4 mm of travel at the 1.5 m/s drive limit.
# │ How:     AISLE.perception_age and RM.base.max_velocity; displacement via
# │          calc_spatial_information_age_displacement.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class RackEndOpeningAge:
    """Travel during the navigation camera's observation age at the drive limit."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age  # category: derived
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    dx = calc_spatial_information_age_displacement(v, t_age).to(ureg.millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_age.to(millisecond).magnitude - 51.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected t_age: {t_age}")
    check(abs(v.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected drive limit: {v}")
    check(abs(dx.magnitude - 77.4) < 0.05, f"Unexpected travel during t_age: {dx}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v.to(meter / second), unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    dx_str = fmt_length(dx, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
```

Every motion executed by a physical AI system rests on a claim about the physical world derived from earlier sensor readings. Perception converts raw energy incident on a detector—photons hitting a CMOS sensor array, laser pulses reflected to an avalanche photodiode, or elastomeric deformation at a mechanical fingertip—into concrete spatial claims: the volume occupied by a human coworker, the metric range to a storage rack upright, or the incipient slip of a grasped object. Machine perception has historically been evaluated using static recognition accuracy on fixed benchmarks, where a model scoring high precision on an image is rewarded regardless of when the exposure occurred or how the camera was moving. For an embodied machine, that abstraction collapses. A spatial claim can safely support motion only if it explicitly specifies three properties: the instant its energy was captured, the coordinate frame in which it was measured, and a rigorous bound on its spatial uncertainty. Evaluated against the machine's current velocity, this qualified uncertainty must remain within the remaining physical clearance.

Validating that physical margin requires tracing the evidence pipeline from physical transduction to motion qualification. Sensing modalities must first be matched to the exact physical quantities an action requires, followed by calibration and detector physics that ground the measurement in space and time. Latency must be strictly budgeted from photon capture to observation dispatch, bounding spatial uncertainty against silent sensor corruption before downstream safety filters permit motion. Perception concludes once it yields a qualified measurement; synthesizing these discrete measurements across time into persistent spatial state is the domain of state estimation and spatial memory (@sec-memory).

While the evaluation record of @sec-evaluation establishes the operational envelope where a learned proposer demonstrates competence, executing that policy requires fresh, verifiable evidence describing the robot and its operating environment. Perception delivers this runtime evidence as dated spatial claims across the proposal boundary (@sec-boundary-machine-model). Crucially, perception executes within the non-deterministic Brain above this boundary and possesses zero actuator authority. Actuator control remains strictly governed by the deterministic permission path below the boundary, which evaluates proposed actions against the capture timestamps, coordinate frames, and error qualifications attached to each perceptual claim.

The warehouse mobile manipulator illustrates how dramatically dataset recognition metrics can diverge from real-time utility. A vision model might detect an individual stepping past a rack upright with near-perfect benchmark accuracy, yet still provide the trajectory planner with an obsolete obstacle position. The physical environment continues to move while the navigation camera integrates charge, serializes pixel rows across the bus, and runs inference through the vision pipeline. On this mobile manipulator, `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.t_age_str` elapses between the midpoint of optical exposure and the dispatch of the processed observation (derived in the latency waterfall of @sec-perception-latency-waterfall). Driving at its `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.v_str` velocity limit, the mobile base covers `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.dx_str` over that single observation interval. Benchmark accuracy reveals nothing about whether an observation remains sufficiently fresh to guarantee safe clearance. In embodied AI systems, every observation carries an expiration date.

Whether an architecture employs an end-to-end vision-language-action (VLA) policy [@brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla], an end-to-end visuomotor model without a language backbone [@zhao2023learning], or a modular estimator, it must reconcile the physical scene captured at a past instant with the kinematic state of the robot at execution. Architectural choices alter processing latency and representation formats, but no network topology can bypass photon integration, sensor readout, or bus transport delay. Explicit timestamps and spatial transforms keep this spatiotemporal relationship inspectable and auditable; latent representations require external instrumentation and supervisory monitors. Crucially, neither architectural approach can convert ambiguous sensor signals into ground truth: a specular reflection on a polished warehouse floor remains an optical hazard regardless of model capacity.

Navigating past a blind rack corner requires establishing a bounded occupied volume in the robot's base coordinate frame before available stopping distance is exhausted. RGB appearance helps classify an object as a person, but monocular bearing alone cannot supply metric range. The navigation camera therefore requires corroborated depth measurements before its detections can justify motion clearance. At the end-effector, sensing requirements change completely: while external optical cameras guide the initial reaching approach, detecting contact mechanics, shear forces, and incipient slip requires tactile sensing directly at the fingertips. Sensor selection begins by identifying the physical quantity governing each action, followed by analyzing sensor coverage, update rates, and environmental failure modes.

The comparison in @tbl-08-sensor-modalities summarizes the physical evidence each sensing mechanism provides, alongside the primary failure modes and safety-critical checks required before fusing claims across an embodied sensor suite. Incorporating a secondary modality mitigates a shared failure mode only when its independent spatial coverage, timing guarantees, extrinsic calibration, and correlated failure risks are established.

| Modality         | Direct physical information                                                | Main limitation                                                                               | Permission-relevant check                             |
|:-----------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------|
| RGB camera       | Bearing, appearance, and image motion                                      | Monocular depth scale is ambiguous; glare, darkness, and occlusion can hide objects           | Fresh capture time and validated metric corroboration |
| Active stereo    | Disparity-derived range with infrared texture projection                   | Sunlight washes out projected pattern; range error grows quadratically with distance ($z^2$)  | Range-dependent residual and bias validation          |
| Structured light | High-density triangulated depth from projected coded patterns              | Ambient solar infrared flooding; multi-robot pattern crosstalk; short range ($<3\,\text{m}$)  | Lighting lux limits and pattern decoding integrity    |
| Time-of-flight   | Metric depth via phase delay (iToF) or photon arrival timing (dToF)        | iToF phase wrapping; multipath reflections in corners; flying pixels on moving edges          | Ambiguity distance and corner multipath flags         |
| Pulsed LiDAR     | Metric time-of-flight range at sampled laser beam directions               | Near-field aerosol backscatter in fog/rain; retroreflector blooming; specular puddle dropouts | Qualified range, return quality, and scan timing      |
| FMCW radar       | Metric range and instantaneous radial Doppler velocity of targets          | Multipath ghost returns off ground; lower angular resolution; antenna sidelobe clutter        | Track association and coverage of crossing targets    |
| Event camera     | Asynchronous per-pixel log-intensity contrast events ($\ge C_{\text{th}}$) | Unchanging scenes supply little event evidence; noise and flicker can still generate events   | Event-rate health and independent metric depth source |
| Optical tactile  | Contact micro-depth, surface normals, and shear force vectors              | Zero sensing before physical contact; strictly localized to gripper elastomeric pad           | Contact threshold, slip flags, and marker tracking    |

: **Spatial sensor modality comparison**: Sensor mechanisms provide complementary but fallible claims across physical operating regimes. Numeric range, accuracy, refresh, and link budgets require a named device and mode. For example, [Prophesee EVT2](https://docs.prophesee.ai/stable/data/encoding_formats/evt2.html) encodes an event in 32 bits, so an event camera's link load scales with its event rate before transport overhead. {#tbl-08-sensor-modalities tbl-colwidths="[15,28,31,26]"}

On an operational robot, this division of responsibility is explicit and reflects established industrial safety engineering. The certified safety claim regarding an obstacle at the rack end belongs neither to the vision model nor to the spinning LiDAR. ISO 3691-4 mandates that an autonomous industrial truck detect persons in its path at Performance Level d (PL d) [@iso3691part4; @tuv2021iso3691], the second highest of the five reliability grades (a through e) defined in ISO 13849-1 [@iso13849part1]. Mobile bases satisfy this mandate using an industrial safety laser scanner—a dual-channel, planar time-of-flight sensor certified as an active opto-electronic protective device under IEC 61496-3 [@iec61496part3; @keyence2026szv]. By design and certification standards, the safety scanner performs no semantic classification; it reports solely whether an opaque object has entered its protective optical field, directly triggering the certified emergency stop circuit described in @sec-enforcement-composite-budget.

The mobile base's spinning LiDAR (an Ouster OS1-64) carries no functional safety rating; its datasheet certifies only electrical, laser, and electromagnetic compatibility [@ouster2025os1]. Instead, it provides the dense 3D metric range field that the software permission path evaluates against spatial clearance limits. This evaluation forms an unrated admission check within the software stack—a protective layer operating above the certified hardware safety floor (@sec-enforcement-certified-functions). Its architectural role is to keep learned proposals smooth and proactive, adjusting trajectories well before the robot approaches the safety scanner's protective boundary and causes an abrupt hardware stop.

Meanwhile, the navigation camera enriches the learned proposer with semantic context: distinguishing a coworker from a stationary tote and predicting velocity headings. Because the proposer constructs its trajectory predictions relative to the camera frame, that image frame's capture timestamp defines the evidence epoch carried by the resulting motion proposal. Synchronizing and cross-dating the high-rate LiDAR stream against this camera epoch is detailed in @sec-perception-lidar-age. Anchoring downstream motion to perceptual data elevates exposure intervals, sensor readout timing, and spatial calibration into load-bearing systems invariants. When operational conditions shift, alternative modalities become essential: active illumination resolves textureless surfaces, event cameras preserve high-speed edge transitions across wide dynamic ranges, and tactile arrays provide the localized contact dynamics that remote optical sensors cannot observe.
## Capture Physics and Calibration {#sec-perception-transduction-calibration}

The navigation camera begins measuring a physical obstacle—such as a warehouse rack upright—the moment photons hit its detector. From initial optical transduction at the silicon photodiode array to the eventual consumption of features by a neural policy backbone or state observer, every intermediate processing stage contributes to the observation age. In CMOS active-pixel sensors, incident photons generate electron-hole pairs through the photoelectric effect according to a wavelength-dependent quantum efficiency $\eta(\lambda)$. Silicon photodiodes accumulate this photocharge across a finite exposure interval $t_{\text{exp}}$, collecting total charge:
$$Q = \int_0^{t_{\text{exp}}} \frac{q \eta(\lambda)}{h \nu} P_{\text{opt}}(t)\,dt$$
where $q$ is the elementary charge, $h$ is Planck's constant, $\nu$ is optical frequency, and $P_{\text{opt}}(t)$ is incident optical power. Photons striking the photodiode array do not instantly register as embeddings in downstream memory. Exposure integration, readout serialization, bus transport across PCIe or MIPI CSI, memory staging, preprocessing kernels, and neural backbone inference each consume a slice of the end-to-end latency budget.

Because the photodiode accumulates charge over the finite exposure duration $t_{\text{exp}}$, the captured frame integrates scene radiance over time while both the robot and the surrounding environment are in motion. Assuming approximately constant linear velocity $\mathbf{v}$ and angular velocity $\boldsymbol{\omega}$, with the optical center displaced from the vehicle's center of rotation by lever arm $\mathbf{r}$, a conservative bound on the physical displacement of the camera center during exposure is:
$$\Delta x_{\text{motion}} = \|\mathbf{v}\| \, t_{\text{exp}} + \|\boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{r}\| \, t_{\text{exp}}$$
This distance measures the physical displacement of the camera center, not the pixel footprint of the blur on the detector plane. Projecting this displacement into image pixels requires scene depth, focal length, viewing direction, and relative attitude changes. Pure rotational motion can smear the image severely even when the camera center remains completely stationary. The resulting **motion blur** acts as a low-pass spatial filter, attenuating image gradients and destroying high-frequency edge information before neural feature extraction or corner detection can run. Downstream estimators can use accurate timestamps and extrinsic calibrations to position the blurred observation at its capture epoch, but no coordinate transformation can synthesize geometric detail lost during optical integration.

The finite integration window also determines which physical instant the resulting image represents. Under an idealized linear sensor response, the pixel value reflects incoming scene radiance $I(t)$ integrated across the exposure window:
$$I_{\text{pixel}} = \int_{0}^{t_{\text{exp}}} I(t)\,dt$$

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-rolling-shutter-skew
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ROLLING-SHUTTER SKEW ON THE NAVIGATION CAMERA
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The exposure paragraph and the rolling-shutter example of
# │          @sec-perception-transduction-calibration.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size the exposure-midpoint lag, per-row blur, and scanline skew
# │          the navigation camera records while the base passes a vertical
# │          rack upright.
# │ Show:    an 8 ms midpoint lag; 3,040 rows in 16.6 ms (5.46 us per row);
# │          24.9 mm of along-track skew and 24 mm of blur at the 1.5 m/s
# │          drive limit, about half of the along-travel allowance delta_loc;
# │          9.1 mm of lateral skew from an illustrative 0.5 rad/s yaw at the
# │          1.10 m rack-end distance, about 6 percent of the side clearance.
# │ How:     RM.nav_camera readout, exposure (a configured setting), and row
# │          count; RM.base drive limit; AISLE.delta_loc, AISLE.d_clear,
# │          AISLE.side_clearance; RM.imu sample rate for compensation.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_frequency, fmt_int, fmt_percent, fmt_display_math, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class RollingShutterSkew:
    """Scanline skew and blur on the running machine's navigation camera at the drive limit."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    camera = RM.nav_camera  # category: datasheet (registry: navigation camera)
    rows = camera.resolution_height  # category: datasheet
    t_readout = camera.readout_time.to(millisecond)  # category: datasheet
    t_exp = camera.exposure_time.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen (configured exposure; low-light worst case, not a sensor rating)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity.to(meter / second)  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    omega_yaw = 0.5 * radian / second  # category: illustrative (yaw rate while turning into the aisle)
    z_upright = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (range to the rack-end upright)
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative (along-travel localization allowance)
    side_clearance = AISLE.side_clearance  # category: illustrative
    f_imu = RM.imu.sample_rate  # category: datasheet
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle.to(meter / second)  # category: chosen (aisle speed, below the derived ceiling)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_exp_half = (t_exp / 2).to(millisecond)
    t_row = (t_readout / rows).to(microsecond)
    skew = (v * t_readout).to(ureg.millimeter)  # along the direction of travel
    blur = (v * t_exp).to(ureg.millimeter)
    skew_over_loc = (skew / delta_loc).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    lateral = (z_upright * omega_yaw.to(1 / second).magnitude * t_readout.to(second).magnitude).to(ureg.millimeter)
    lateral_share = (lateral / side_clearance).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    skew_aisle = (v_aisle * t_readout).to(ureg.millimeter)  # sensitivity: the chosen aisle speed
    skew_aisle_over_loc = (skew_aisle / delta_loc).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(rows == 3040, f"Unexpected navigation-camera row count: {rows}")
    check(abs(t_row.magnitude - 5.46) < 0.005, f"Unexpected row interval: {t_row}")
    check(abs(skew.magnitude - 24.9) < 0.05, f"Unexpected rolling-shutter skew: {skew}")
    check(abs(blur.magnitude - 24.0) < 0.05, f"Unexpected per-row blur: {blur}")
    check(abs(t_exp_half.magnitude - 8.0) < 0.05, f"Unexpected exposure-midpoint lag: {t_exp_half}")
    check(0.45 < skew_over_loc < 0.55, f"Prose says the along-track skew is about half of delta_loc: {skew_over_loc}")
    check(abs(lateral.magnitude - 9.1) < 0.05, f"Unexpected lateral skew from yaw: {lateral}")
    check(0.055 < lateral_share < 0.065, f"Prose says the lateral skew is about 6 percent of the side clearance: {lateral_share}")
    check(abs(skew_aisle.magnitude - 21.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected skew at the aisle speed: {skew_aisle}")
    check(0.4 < skew_aisle_over_loc < 0.45, f"Notebook says the aisle speed still spends over two fifths of delta_loc: {skew_aisle_over_loc}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    rows_str = fmt_int(rows)
    last_row_str = fmt_int(rows - 1)
    t_readout_str = fmt_latency(t_readout, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_exp_str = fmt_latency(t_exp, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_exp_half_str = fmt_latency(t_exp_half, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_row_str = fmt_latency(t_row, unit=microsecond, precision=2)
    skew_str = fmt_length(skew, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    blur_str = fmt_length(blur, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    omega_yaw_str = fmt(omega_yaw.to(radian / second).magnitude, precision=1)
    z_upright_str = fmt_length(z_upright.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(delta_loc.to(ureg.millimeter), unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    lateral_str = fmt_length(lateral, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    lateral_pct_str = fmt_percent(lateral_share, precision=1)
    side_clearance_str = fmt_length(side_clearance.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    f_imu_str = fmt_frequency(f_imu, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0, commas=True)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    skew_aisle_str = fmt_length(skew_aisle, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    skew_aisle_pct_str = fmt_percent(skew_aisle_over_loc, precision=1)

    # Display arithmetic for nbk-perception-readout-shear (magnitudes, LaTeX units)
    _tr = fmt(t_readout.magnitude, precision=1)
    _v = fmt(v.magnitude, precision=1)
    _z = fmt(z_upright.to(meter).magnitude, precision=2)
    _w = fmt(omega_yaw.to(radian / second).magnitude, precision=1)
    _rows = fmt_int(rows, commas=False)
    t_row_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"t_{{\text{{row}}}} = \frac{{t_{{\text{{readout}}}}}}{{H}} = \frac{{{_tr}\ \text{{ms}}}}{{{_rows}}} = {fmt(t_row.magnitude, precision=2)}\ \mu\text{{s}}"
    )
    skew_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\Delta x = v\,t_{{\text{{readout}}}} = {_v}\ \text{{m/s}} \times {_tr}\ \text{{ms}} = {fmt(skew.magnitude, precision=1)}\ \text{{mm}}, \quad \frac{{\Delta x}}{{\delta_{{\text{{loc}}}}}} = \frac{{{fmt(skew.magnitude, precision=1)}\ \text{{mm}}}}{{{fmt(delta_loc.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude, precision=0)}\ \text{{mm}}}} = {fmt(skew_over_loc, precision=2)}"
    )
    lateral_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\Delta y = z\,\omega\,t_{{\text{{readout}}}} = {_z}\ \text{{m}} \times {_w}\ \text{{rad/s}} \times {_tr}\ \text{{ms}} = {fmt(lateral.magnitude, precision=1)}\ \text{{mm}}, \quad \frac{{{fmt(lateral.magnitude, precision=1)}\ \text{{mm}}}}{{{fmt(side_clearance.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude, precision=0)}\ \text{{mm}}}} = {fmt(lateral_share, precision=3)}"
    )
```

Because charge accumulates continuously across this entire window, the effective capture epoch of the resulting image is its exposure midpoint: exactly $t_{\text{exp}}/2$ after the shutter opens and $t_{\text{exp}}/2$ before it closes. For the mobile base running at its `{python} RollingShutterSkew.v_str` drive limit with the navigation camera configured to a `{python} RollingShutterSkew.t_exp_str` exposure, the frame represents the scene where the robot was `{python} RollingShutterSkew.t_exp_half_str` earlier, while the robot traverses `{python} RollingShutterSkew.blur_str` of translation during the exposure itself. Exposure time is a configured software parameter rather than an immutable hardware constant. Our warehouse mobile manipulator configures this relatively long exposure to operate reliably in dim aisle lighting; higher ambient illumination permits shorter integration times, scaling down both motion blur and midpoint latency proportionally.

### Rolling shutter distortion and motion compensation

How exposure is scheduled across the pixel array determines the fundamental geometric consistency of the image. In a **global shutter**\index{Global shutter!definition} sensor, every photodiode integrates charge during the exact same temporal window and transfers accumulated electrons to shielded in-pixel storage nodes simultaneously. In contrast, cost and silicon die area constraints often dictate the use of a **rolling shutter**\index{Rolling shutter!definition} sensor, where rows are reset, exposed, and read out sequentially from top to bottom ($y = 0$ to $y = H - 1$). Each successive scanline begins its exposure after an incremental row readout period $t_{\text{row}}$, introducing a progressive time skew across the vertical axis:
$$t(y) = t_{\text{start}} + y \cdot t_{\text{row}}$$
where $t_{\text{start}}$ denotes the exposure start time of the initial row ($y = 0$). When the vehicle translates at linear velocity $v$ perpendicular to a vertical object, scanline $y$ samples that object at an along-track spatial offset:
$$\Delta x(y) = v \cdot y \cdot t_{\text{row}}$$ {#eq-percep-rolling-shutter-skew}

Under angular motion, rolling shutter distortion becomes non-linear. If the camera rotates with angular velocity vector $\boldsymbol{\omega} = [\omega_x, \omega_y, \omega_z]^\top$ (for example, rapid yaw or pitch during aggressive vehicle maneuvers), the camera attitude drifts continuously throughout the readout phase. The optical axis points in a slightly different direction for every single scanline. For a row at vertical coordinate $y$, the incremental rotation relative to the start of the frame is approximately $\Delta \boldsymbol{\theta}(y) \approx \boldsymbol{\omega} \cdot y \cdot t_{\text{row}}$. This line-dependent rotation bends straight structural lines into curves, stretches or compresses vertical scale during pitching motions, and shears vertical surfaces into inclined planes, as photographed on the rotating propeller blades in @fig-rolling-shutter-skew.

Consider the warehouse mobile manipulator navigating past a vertical rack upright at its `{python} RollingShutterSkew.v_str` drive limit. A vertical post that spans the full frame height does not appear vertical in the raw pixel array, because the sensor reads the bottom scanline ($y =$ `{python} RollingShutterSkew.last_row_str`) an entire readout cycle after the top scanline ($y = 0$). This delay induces two distinct geometric errors that consume separate safety margins: along-track translation shears the upright along the direction of travel, while base yaw during a turn shifts the feature laterally. Notebook \ref{nbk-perception-readout-shear} quantifies both effects.

::: {#nbk-perception-readout-shear .callout-notebook title="The readout shear"}

**Problem**: The base passes a rack upright at its drive limit while turning into the aisle. How far apart does the navigation camera record the upright's top and bottom rows, and what share of the clearance each error spends does it use?

**Variables**:

* Rows $H =$ `{python} RollingShutterSkew.rows_str` and readout $t_{\text{readout}} =$ `{python} RollingShutterSkew.t_readout_str` (Datasheet, full-resolution mode).
* Drive limit $v =$ `{python} RollingShutterSkew.v_str` (Illustrative).
* Yaw rate $\omega =$ `{python} RollingShutterSkew.omega_yaw_str` rad/s while turning into the aisle, at the rack-end range $z =$ `{python} RollingShutterSkew.z_upright_str` (Illustrative).
* Localization allowance $\delta_{\text{loc}} =$ `{python} RollingShutterSkew.delta_loc_str` and side clearance `{python} RollingShutterSkew.side_clearance_str` (Illustrative; @tbl-01-machine-card).

**Math**:

*Row interval.*
`{python} RollingShutterSkew.t_row_math`

*Along-track skew.* At the last row, @eq-percep-rolling-shutter-skew gives
`{python} RollingShutterSkew.skew_math`

*Lateral skew.* The bearing rotates by $\omega\,t_{\text{readout}}$ during readout, which moves the upright sideways at range $z$ by
`{python} RollingShutterSkew.lateral_math`

*Sensitivity.* At the aisle's chosen `{python} RollingShutterSkew.v_aisle_str`, the along-track skew is still `{python} RollingShutterSkew.skew_aisle_str`, `{python} RollingShutterSkew.skew_aisle_pct_str` percent of $\delta_{\text{loc}}$.

**Result**: The bottom rows see the upright from a camera position `{python} RollingShutterSkew.skew_str` farther down the aisle than the top rows did, half of $\delta_{\text{loc}}$. Yaw adds `{python} RollingShutterSkew.lateral_str` sideways, about `{python} RollingShutterSkew.lateral_pct_str` percent of the side clearance.

**Systems insight**: Uncorrected, one readout would spend half of the localization allowance that the stopping budget holds for the whole state estimate, and slowing to aisle speed barely helps. The budget's $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ is therefore valid only if the skew is removed before the estimator sees the frame. The lateral term is small at the rack end, but it grows with range and turn rate, so it belongs in the calibration and timing checks rather than in a budget row.

:::

The along-track error charges directly against $\delta_{\text{loc}}$: treating the image as an instantaneous rigid perspective projection mistakenly models the bottom of the upright as closer along the corridor than the top, directly consuming the along-travel stopping allowance. Both error components scale linearly with total readout time. A global-shutter sensor, such as the wrist-mounted camera on our robot's manipulator arm, eliminates scanline skew at the expense of larger pixel pitch and higher silicon cost. Selecting a shutter architecture is therefore a primary systems decision whenever a sensor's measurements inform clearance boundaries. We deliberately equip the mobile base with a rolling-shutter navigation camera to explore this challenging systems constraint. Resolving this spatial artifact requires **rolling-shutter motion compensation**\index{Rolling-shutter motion compensation!definition}: unwarping image coordinates geometrically using an interpolated camera pose for every scanline. The onboard IMU supplies high-rate (`{python} RollingShutterSkew.f_imu_str`) angular velocity and specific-force[^fn-imu-specific-force] samples rather than direct velocity measurements. A fused state estimator integrates these inertial readings with bias estimates, gravity tracking, and wheel odometry to compute continuous body poses. Transforming these poses through calibrated body-to-camera extrinsics yields the exact optical pose for each scanline, allowing the perception pipeline to rectify the image before running stereo matching or landmark triangulation.

[^fn-imu-specific-force]: **Specific Force**: An accelerometer measures non-gravitational acceleration, $\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{g}$, so a unit resting on the floor reads one $g$ upward and one in free fall reads zero. Dead reckoning must therefore subtract gravity through an attitude estimate, and an attitude error $\theta$ leaks $g\sin\theta$ into horizontal acceleration, which integrates twice into the per-row poses that de-skewing relies on. \index{Inertial measurement unit!specific force}

@Fig-08-rolling-shutter-rows plots this along-travel sampling progression against sensor row index (zero at the top) and read time: the solid line charts the camera advancing by `{python} RollingShutterSkew.skew_str` down the aisle between the top and bottom rows at `{python} RollingShutterSkew.v_str`, enclosed within a `{python} RollingShutterSkew.blur_str` shaded motion-blur band. The dashed vertical boundary marks `{python} RollingShutterSkew.delta_loc_str` of localization allowance, demonstrating that uncorrected scanline skew alone consumes approximately half of the vehicle's total state-estimation budget.

::: {#fig-08-rolling-shutter-rows fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Row-by-row sampling on the navigation camera**: At the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.v_str` drive limit, each of the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.rows_str` rows is read `{python} RollingShutterSkew.t_row_str` after the one above it, so the bottom row sees the rack upright from a camera position `{python} RollingShutterSkew.skew_str` farther down the aisle than the top row (solid line; upper axis gives the read time). The shaded band is each row's own motion blur, `{python} RollingShutterSkew.blur_str` over the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.t_exp_str` exposure. Uncorrected, the skew alone spends about half of the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.delta_loc_str` localization allowance (dashed line)." fig-alt="Line plot with image row on the vertical axis, zero at the top, and camera position along the direction of travel in millimeters on the horizontal axis, with read time in milliseconds on a second axis above. A straight line runs from zero at the top row to about 25 millimeters at the bottom row, inside a shaded band about 24 millimeters wide. A dashed vertical line at 50 millimeters marks the localization allowance."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-perception-rolling-shutter-rows
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ROLLING-SHUTTER ROW SAMPLING (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-08-rolling-shutter-rows in
# │          @sec-perception-transduction-calibration.
# │
# │ Goal:    Make the along-travel skew physical: row index against the camera
# │          position at which that row was read, with per-row blur and the
# │          localization allowance it spends.
# │ Show:    0 -> 24.9 mm over 3,040 rows (16.6 ms); 24 mm blur band; 50 mm
# │          delta_loc line.
# │ How:     Reads RollingShutterSkew only; the plotted endpoint is guarded
# │          against its skew.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.fmt import check

RS = RollingShutterSkew
PETROL, PINE, SOFT = "#007A87", "#1A4D3E", "#4A5568"  # measured, structural, neutral (theme-colors.tex)

# ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
n_rows = RS.rows
v_mm_per_ms = RS.v.to(ureg.millimeter / millisecond).magnitude
t_row_ms = RS.t_row.to(millisecond).magnitude
blur_mm = RS.blur.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude
dloc_mm = RS.delta_loc.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
rows_axis = np.array([0.0, n_rows - 1.0])
x_cam = v_mm_per_ms * t_row_ms * rows_axis

# ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(v_mm_per_ms * t_row_ms * n_rows - RS.skew.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-6, "The plotted skew must equal v * t_readout.")
check(RS.skew.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude < dloc_mm, "The skew must sit inside the drawn allowance.")

# ┌── 4. PLOT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(5.2, 2.7))
ax.fill_betweenx(rows_axis, x_cam - blur_mm / 2, x_cam + blur_mm / 2, color=PETROL, alpha=0.14, lw=0)
ax.plot(x_cam, rows_axis, color=PETROL, lw=2.0)
ax.axvline(dloc_mm, color=PINE, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (4, 3)))
ax.text(dloc_mm - 1, n_rows * 0.08, rf"$\delta_{{\mathrm{{loc}}}}$ = {RS.delta_loc_str}", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=8, color=PINE)
ax.annotate(
    f"skew {RS.skew_str}",
    xy=(x_cam[-1], rows_axis[-1]),
    xytext=(x_cam[-1] + 6, n_rows * 0.72),
    fontsize=8,
    color=PETROL,
    va="center",
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=SOFT, lw=0.6),
)
ax.text(-blur_mm / 2 + 0.5, n_rows * 0.18, f"blur {RS.blur_str}", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=8, color=SOFT)
ax.set_xlim(-blur_mm / 2 - 2, dloc_mm + 6)
ax.set_ylim(n_rows * 1.03, -n_rows * 0.03)
ax.set_xlabel("camera position along travel when the row is read (mm)", fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylabel("image row", fontsize=9)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
top = ax.secondary_xaxis("top", functions=(lambda x: x / v_mm_per_ms, lambda t: t * v_mm_per_ms))
top.set_xlabel("read time after the top row (ms)", fontsize=9)
top.tick_params(labelsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

::: {#fig-rolling-shutter-skew fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Rolling shutter distortion geometry**: A phone camera's rolling shutter photographs a turning aircraft propeller. Because scanlines are exposed and read sequentially from top to bottom rather than simultaneously, blades that move appreciably during the frame's readout are recorded as curved, disconnected arcs; each row samples the blade at a later instant. On a moving robot the same row-by-row sampling shears straight structures and biases the geometry downstream estimators triangulate. (Credit: [Dick Lyon](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Propellor_with_rolling-shutter_artifact.jpg) / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0)." fig-alt="Photograph from an aircraft window of a propeller and engine nacelle in flight, with sky and ground below. The blades appear as bent, curved shapes, some detached from the hub, instead of straight radial blades."}
![](images/jpg/fig08_real_rolling_shutter_skew.jpg){width="85%"}
:::

The curved, detached propeller blade segments photographed in @fig-rolling-shutter-skew capture why geometric unwarping must precede spatial interpretation: because scanlines are exposed and read sequentially down the sensor rather than simultaneously, rapid motion shears radial structures across scanline rows. Learned feature backbones can readily misinterpret row-by-row shear as intrinsic physical geometry, while classical stereo matchers fail when scanline displacement shifts correspondences off the calibrated epipolar line.[^fn-epipolar-stereo-geometry] Scaling up model capacity cannot compensate for uncorrected physical sampling distortion; the network simply learns biased geometric representations.

[^fn-epipolar-stereo-geometry]: **Epipolar Line**: For a calibrated camera pair, a point seen in one image can appear in the other only along one line, the projection of the ray from the first camera's center through that point (@sec-perception-error-clearance derives it). Stereo matchers search that line alone, so a rolling-shutter shear that moves a correspondence even one row off it produces a mismatch rather than a slightly worse match. \index{Epipolar geometry!rolling-shutter mismatch}

### Camera calibration

Rolling-shutter compensation assumes that the camera's geometry is already known, and every metric claim the camera supports rests on that calibration. Under the **pinhole camera model**\index{Pinhole camera model} [@hartley2003multiple], the intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$ maps a point $\mathbf{P}_c = [X_c, Y_c, Z_c]^\top$ in the camera's optical frame to the pixel $[u, v]^\top$:
$$\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \sim \frac{1}{Z_c} \mathbf{K} \mathbf{P}_c = \frac{1}{Z_c} \begin{bmatrix} f_x & 0 & c_x \\ 0 & f_y & c_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X_c \\ Y_c \\ Z_c \end{bmatrix}$$ {#eq-percep-pinhole-projection}
where $f_x, f_y$ are focal lengths in pixels and $(c_x, c_y)$ is the principal point. Inverting the map recovers only a bearing ray, along which every depth is consistent with the pixel:
$$\mathbf{r}(u, v) = \mathbf{K}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{u - c_x}{f_x} \\ \frac{v - c_y}{f_y} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ {#eq-percep-bearing-ray}

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-capture-timing-scale
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CAPTURE-TIMING AND ATTITUDE ERROR SCALES AT THE RACK END
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The bearing-ray paragraph of
# │          @sec-perception-transduction-calibration and the hardware-trigger
# │          paragraph of @sec-perception-handoff.
# │
# │ Goal:    Put machine-scale numbers on timing and attitude errors: travel per
# │          millisecond of misdating, lateral error per degree at the rack end,
# │          the travel hidden by an uncorrected exposure-start trigger stamp,
# │          and the lateral error per millisecond of stamp jitter while turning.
# │ Show:    1.5 mm per ms; 19.2 mm per degree at 1.10 m; 8 ms and 12 mm for
# │          the trigger correction; 0.5 mrad and 0.55 mm per ms of jitter.
# │ How:     RM.base drive limit; AISLE.d_clear; RM.nav_camera exposure;
# │          the illustrative yaw rate of RollingShutterSkew.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_angle, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class CaptureTimingScale:
    """Machine-scale travel and lever-arm errors from timing and attitude offsets."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity.to(meter / second)  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    z = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (rack-end distance)
    t_exp = RM.nav_camera.exposure_time.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen (configured exposure)
    omega_yaw = RollingShutterSkew.omega_yaw  # category: illustrative (yaw rate)
    dt_unit = 1.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (one millisecond of error)
    theta_unit = 1.0 * ureg.degree  # category: illustrative (one degree of error)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    dx_per_ms = (v * dt_unit).to(ureg.millimeter)
    dy_per_deg = (z * math.sin(theta_unit.to(radian).magnitude)).to(ureg.millimeter)
    t_trigger_corr = (t_exp / 2).to(millisecond)
    dx_trigger = (v * t_trigger_corr).to(ureg.millimeter)
    dtheta_per_ms = (omega_yaw * dt_unit).to(ureg.milliradian)
    dy_per_ms_jitter = (z * dtheta_per_ms.to(radian).magnitude).to(ureg.millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(dx_per_ms.magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected travel per ms: {dx_per_ms}")
    check(abs(dy_per_deg.magnitude - 19.2) < 0.05, f"Unexpected lateral error per degree: {dy_per_deg}")
    check(abs(dx_trigger.magnitude - 12.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected trigger-correction travel: {dx_trigger}")
    check(abs(dy_per_ms_jitter.magnitude - 0.55) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected lateral error per ms of jitter: {dy_per_ms_jitter}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    z_str = fmt_length(z.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    dx_per_ms_str = fmt_length(dx_per_ms, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    dy_per_deg_str = fmt_length(dy_per_deg, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    t_trigger_corr_str = fmt_latency(t_trigger_corr, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    dx_trigger_str = fmt_length(dx_trigger, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    dtheta_per_ms_str = fmt_angle(dtheta_per_ms, unit=ureg.milliradian, precision=1)
    dy_per_ms_jitter_str = fmt_length(dy_per_ms_jitter, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
```

This bearing ray emanates from the camera's optical center at the precise instant of photon capture $t_0$. If downstream motion planning unprojects $\mathbf{r}(u, v)$ using the robot's *current* pose instead of its historical capture pose, the elapsed observation age $t_{\text{age}}$ translates the ray origin by $\Delta \mathbf{x} = \int_{t_0}^{t_0+t_{\text{age}}} \mathbf{v}(t)\,dt$. These timing and angular errors scale along entirely different physical axes. At our `{python} CaptureTimingScale.v_str` drive limit, each millisecond of unmodeled latency shifts the ray origin by `{python} CaptureTimingScale.dx_per_ms_str`, making a total observation age of `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.t_age_str` displace the origin by `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.dx_str`. Conversely, attitude errors scale with range: a single degree of orientation misalignment shifts a target at the `{python} CaptureTimingScale.z_str` rack-end distance by `{python} CaptureTimingScale.dy_per_deg_str` laterally, expanding proportionally with distance. Unchecked, either discrepancy can push a physical rack upright entirely outside the bounding volume evaluated by the safety checker. A single monocular camera cannot recover metric range along its bearing rays; scale must be supplied by stereo disparity, an active ranging sensor, or a learned geometric prior—each introducing uncertainty that @sec-perception-error-clearance audits against the operating clearance budget. Optical lens distortion is rectified inside the hardware image signal processor (ISP) stage detailed in @tbl-08-latency-budget. We develop the full projection equations, radial-tangential distortion models, and Zhang's planar calibration method [@zhang2000flexible] in @sec-appendix-systems-vision.

Spatial extrinsics and temporal synchronization between the camera and the IMU must be calibrated jointly [@furgale2013unified]. An extrinsic orientation error $\theta$ misplaces an observed feature at depth $z$ by approximately $z\,\theta$, while spatial translation between the camera center and the IMU introduces centripetal and tangential lever-arm accelerations (@sec-appendix-control-spatial). Similarly, an uncalibrated temporal offset $\Delta t$ between image exposure and inertial sampling causes an effective orientation error of $\omega\,\Delta t$ while turning at angular velocity $\omega$. This timing skew displaces the reconstructed feature by approximately $z\,\omega\,\Delta t$, growing with both vehicle yaw rate and target distance. Hardware-latching exposure triggers and IMU clock signals to a shared real-time counter bounds this synchronization offset to sub-microsecond regimes, leaving small residual latencies for online filtering. Because mechanical shocks and thermal expansion degrade calibration over time, every observation packet must record its calibration identifier alongside its empirical operating envelope.

### Choosing metric depth for the aisle

Because a single bearing ray leaves range undetermined, robotic systems often deploy active optical depth sensors to recover scale. However, ambient warehouse lighting, surface material properties, and optical interference from neighboring robot fleets dictate which physical transduction principle remains viable in practice.

**Structured light**\index{Structured light!transduction} projects a known pseudo-random or coded infrared pattern onto the scene and triangulates surface deformation using an offset receiver camera. This active pattern injects distinct visual texture onto featureless cardboard cartons. However, direct sunlight from skylights or open loading docks easily washes out the projected infrared pattern, and overlapping projectors from adjacent mobile bases create optical interference that corrupts feature correspondence. Engineering qualification must evaluate the operating environment under peak ambient lux and multi-robot contention rather than treating structured light as an unconditional depth source.

**Indirect time-of-flight (iToF)**\index{Time-of-flight!indirect vs direct} calculates distance by measuring the phase shift of continuous-wave amplitude-modulated infrared light. While phase differences yield dense range maps with compact hardware, modulation periodicity creates phase wrapping and distance ambiguity intervals. Furthermore, multi-path reflections—ubiquitous in metallic warehouse corners and industrial shelving—cause diffuse photons to traverse multiple bounces, producing severely biased depth estimates. In dynamic scenes, motion between sequential phase sample exposures introduces edge artifacts. **Direct time-of-flight (dToF)** avoids periodic phase wrapping by measuring the arrival times of discrete photon pulses using single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs). Although dToF eliminates phase ambiguity, it remains subject to timing jitter in the receiver discriminator, multi-path contamination, and optical pile-up from high-reflectance foregrounds.

**Active stereo**\index{Active stereo!transduction} combines structured infrared illumination with a calibrated stereo camera pair. Unlike structured light systems that must decode a proprietary pattern, active stereo uses projected speckle purely to synthesize artificial texture on smooth surfaces while computing standard epipolar stereo correspondence. If bright ambient light washes out the infrared pattern, the underlying stereo pipeline continues operating over ambient visible texture. Conversely, if a smooth surface lacks ambient texture, high illumination alone cannot resolve depth. The range-dependent uncertainty analysis in @sec-perception-error-clearance determines whether active stereo depth uncertainty satisfies the robot's required stopping clearance.

### Neuromorphic event cameras and asynchronous temporal contrast

Conventional CMOS sensors integrate photons over a synchronous exposure window, inherently trading motion blur against low-light photon starvation. **Neuromorphic event cameras** (Dynamic Vision Sensors, or DVS)\index{Neuromorphic event cameras!transduction}\index{Event cameras!transduction}[^fn-neuromorphic-retina-origin] abandon discrete frames entirely [@lichtsteiner2008128; @gallego2022event].

[^fn-neuromorphic-retina-origin]: **Neuromorphic**: Carver Mead coined the term at Caltech for analog circuits that compute the way neural tissue does [@mead1990], and the silicon retina built in his group is the ancestor of the Dynamic Vision Sensor [@lichtsteiner2008128]. Like the retina, each pixel reports change rather than level, so an obstacle that stands still in front of a stationary sensor produces no events and is invisible to it. \index{Neuromorphic engineering!origin}

Each pixel on an event sensor array operates autonomously, containing a logarithmic photodiode, an analog amplifier, and two differential voltage comparators. The pixel continuously monitors incoming scene radiance $I(u, v, t)$. Whenever the temporal change in logarithmic intensity exceeds a configurable contrast threshold $C_{\text{th}}$, the pixel emits an asynchronous digital event packet $e_k$:
$$|\Delta \ln I(u, v, t)| = |\ln I(u, v, t) - \ln I(u, v, t_{\text{last}})| \ge C_{\text{th}}$$
$$e_k = \langle u_k, v_k, t_k, p_k \rangle$$
where $(u_k, v_k)$ is the pixel address, $t_k$ is the event timestamp latched with microsecond resolution ($1\text{--}10\,\mu\text{s}$), and $p_k \in \{-1, +1\}$ is the polarity indicating whether radiance increased or decreased.

Event sensing preserves the temporal fidelity of high-speed edge transitions without waiting for a complete exposure cycle and serial scanline readout, providing high temporal resolution for rapid maneuvers. The fundamental systems trade-off lies in the nature of temporal contrast: static obstacles produce zero events when the camera is stationary, rendering unmoving obstacles undetectable without ego-motion. Furthermore, high-frequency fluorescent lighting flicker and thermal noise generate spurious event bursts. The bandwidth demand across the physical sensor interface is therefore dynamic and scene-dependent rather than deterministic and fixed.

Downstream estimation algorithms must convert asynchronous coordinate streams in $(u, v, t)$ space into representations suitable for neural networks or state observers. Accumulating events into fixed time slices allows the use of standard convolutional backbones but reintroduces latency; processing individual event timestamps maintains sub-millisecond temporal responsiveness at the cost of specialized asynchronous graph or spiking architectures. Neither representation provides absolute metric depth without stereo baseline pairing or active sensor fusion.

### Active LiDAR and radar ranging transduction

While optical cameras capture dense angular projections of ambient illumination, active ranging sensors, principally Light Detection and Ranging (**LiDAR**)\index{LiDAR!transduction physics} and Radio Detection and Ranging (**radar**)\index{Radar!FMCW transduction}, emit structured electromagnetic energy and measure its reflection, directly extracting metric depth and radial velocity.

Pulsed time-of-flight LiDAR calculates radial distance $R$ by measuring the round-trip flight duration $\Delta t$ of an emitted laser pulse traveling at the speed of light $c$:
$$R = \frac{c \cdot \Delta t}{2}$$

In three-dimensional space, optical scanners steer each pulse along azimuth $\theta$ and elevation $\phi$, casting an emitted ray along unit direction vector $\mathbf{d}(\theta, \phi) = [\cos\phi\cos\theta, \; \cos\phi\sin\theta, \; \sin\phi]^\top$. When reflected energy trips the receiver threshold after flight time $\Delta t$, the sensor unprojects the return into a 3D point in the sensor frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{lidar}}$ via ray casting (@eq-percep-lidar-ray):
$$\mathbf{p}_{\text{lidar}} = R \cdot \mathbf{d}(\theta, \phi) = \frac{c \cdot \Delta t}{2} \begin{bmatrix} \cos\phi \cos\theta \\ \cos\phi \sin\theta \\ \sin\phi \end{bmatrix}$$ {#eq-percep-lidar-ray}

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-lidar-sweep
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE MACHINE'S LIDAR: RANGE ERROR AND SWEEP DISTORTION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The LiDAR paragraphs of @sec-perception-transduction-calibration;
# │          reused by the LiDAR age budget (the state-estimation example of
# │          @sec-perception-state-estimation re-derives its inputs).
# │
# │ Goal:    Give the OS1-64's datasheet range precision and bias, and size
# │          the motion the base makes during one 20 Hz revolution.
# │ Show:    precision 5-30 mm (1 sigma), accuracy 25 mm; 50 ms sweep; 75 mm
# │          of travel and 25 mrad (1.4 degrees) of yaw across one sweep.
# │ How:     RM.lidar.scan_rate; Ouster OS1 Rev7 datasheet (firmware 3.1)
# │          precision and accuracy (registry), specified in the 1024 x 10 Hz
# │          mode; illustrative yaw rate.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_frequency, fmt_angle, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class LidarSweep:
    """Range error and one-revolution motion distortion for the machine's OS1-64."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    lidar = RM.lidar  # category: datasheet (registry: Ouster OS1-64)
    f_scan = lidar.scan_rate  # category: datasheet (configured 20 Hz mode)
    sigma_r_min = lidar.range_precision_min  # category: datasheet (registry: OS1 Rev7 precision min, 1 sigma, beyond 1 m)
    sigma_r_max = lidar.range_precision_max  # category: datasheet (registry: OS1 Rev7 precision max, 1 sigma, beyond 1 m)
    bias_r = lidar.range_accuracy  # category: datasheet (registry: OS1 Rev7 accuracy, Lambertian targets)
    wavelength = lidar.laser_wavelength  # category: datasheet (registry: OS1 Rev7 laser wavelength)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity.to(meter / second)  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    omega_yaw = 0.5 * radian / second  # category: illustrative (yaw rate)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_sweep = (1 / f_scan).to(millisecond)
    dx_sweep = (v * t_sweep).to(ureg.millimeter)
    dtheta_sweep = (omega_yaw * t_sweep).to(ureg.milliradian)
    dtheta_sweep_deg = dtheta_sweep.to(ureg.degree)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(f_scan.to(ureg.hertz).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected LiDAR scan rate: {f_scan}")
    check(abs(t_sweep.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected sweep period: {t_sweep}")
    check(abs(dx_sweep.magnitude - 75.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected travel per sweep: {dx_sweep}")
    check(abs(dtheta_sweep.magnitude - 25.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected yaw per sweep: {dtheta_sweep}")
    check(wavelength.to(ureg.nanometer).magnitude < 1000, "The OS1-64 emits in the near infrared that silicon detectors sense.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    wavelength_str = fmt(wavelength.to(ureg.nanometer).magnitude, precision=0)
    f_scan_str = fmt_frequency(f_scan, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    sigma_r_min_str = fmt_length(sigma_r_min, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    sigma_r_max_str = fmt_length(sigma_r_max, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    bias_r_str = fmt_length(bias_r, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    t_sweep_str = fmt_latency(t_sweep, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    dx_sweep_str = fmt_length(dx_sweep, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    omega_yaw_str = fmt(omega_yaw.to(radian / second).magnitude, precision=1)
    dtheta_sweep_str = fmt(dtheta_sweep.magnitude, precision=0)
    dtheta_sweep_deg_str = fmt(dtheta_sweep_deg.magnitude, precision=1)
```

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-active-sensor-scales
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ACTIVE-SENSOR RESOLUTION SCALES
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The LiDAR transverse-uncertainty item and the FMCW range-resolution
# │          paragraph of @sec-perception-transduction-calibration.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size the LiDAR spot at range and the FMCW radar range resolution.
# │ Show:    30 m x 2 mrad = 60 mm spot; c / (2 x 4 GHz) = 3.75 cm.
# │ How:     sigma_perp = R * div; Delta R = c / (2 B).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_angle, fmt_length, fmt_frequency, check

class ActiveSensorScales:
    """LiDAR spot size and FMCW range resolution for generic sensors."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    r_spot = 30.0 * meter  # category: illustrative (range for the spot example)
    div = 2.0 * ureg.milliradian  # category: illustrative (generic beam divergence)
    b_chirp = 4.0 * ureg.gigahertz  # category: illustrative (77-81 GHz automotive sweep)
    c_light = (1 * ureg.speed_of_light).to(meter / second)  # category: constant (speed of light)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    spot = (r_spot * div.to(ureg.radian).magnitude).to(ureg.millimeter)
    dr_radar = (c_light / (2 * b_chirp)).to(ureg.centimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(spot.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected LiDAR spot: {spot}")
    check(abs(dr_radar.magnitude - 3.747) < 0.01, f"Unexpected radar range resolution: {dr_radar}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    r_spot_str = fmt_length(r_spot, unit=meter, precision=0)
    div_str = fmt_angle(div, unit=ureg.milliradian, precision=0)
    spot_str = fmt_length(spot, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    b_chirp_str = fmt_frequency(b_chirp, unit=ureg.gigahertz, precision=0)
    dr_radar_str = fmt_length(dr_radar, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=2)
```

Spatial uncertainty in this unprojected 3D point decomposes into two distinct physical mechanisms:

1. **Radial uncertainty ($\sigma_R$)**: Governed by receiver discriminator timing jitter $\sigma_{\Delta t}$ and pulse rise time, $\sigma_R = \frac{c}{2} \sigma_{\Delta t}$ remains approximately constant across operating distances until return signal attenuation drops photon counts near the detection threshold. The manufacturer datasheet for the robot's OS1-64 specifies a one-standard-deviation precision between `{python} LidarSweep.sigma_r_min_str` and `{python} LidarSweep.sigma_r_max_str` beyond 1 m, alongside a systematic accuracy bias of `{python} LidarSweep.bias_r_str` on diffuse targets [@ouster2025os1]. This systematic accuracy figure bounds the bias of the mean—a calibration offset that temporal averaging cannot eliminate.
2. **Transverse uncertainty ($\sigma_\perp$)**: Governed by optical beam divergence $\delta\theta_{\text{div}}$ and internal angular encoder quantization $\sigma_\theta$. The laser pulse expands into a narrow cone rather than propagating along an infinitesimal line. At range $R$, the transverse spot footprint expands as $\sigma_\perp \approx R \cdot \delta\theta_{\text{div}}$. At $R =$ `{python} ActiveSensorScales.r_spot_str`, an illustrative `{python} ActiveSensorScales.div_str` beam divergence illuminates a `{python} ActiveSensorScales.spot_str` circular disk. When this footprint strikes a surface boundary, the detector receives mixed returns from both foreground and background, elongating spatial uncertainty ellipsoids orthogonal to the line of sight and blurring geometric edges.

Most terrestrial systems operate either at near-infrared wavelengths below $1{,}000\,\text{nm}$, where silicon detectors respond, or at an eye-safe $1{,}550\,\text{nm}$ (permitting higher pulse energies under IEC 60825-1 Class 1 laser regulations).[^fn-laser-class1-safety] The machine's OS1-64 is of the first kind: it emits at `{python} LidarSweep.wavelength_str` nm as a Class 1 laser product [@ouster2025os1]. Mechanical spinning LiDAR systems rotate an array of 16 to 128 laser diodes and avalanche photodiode (APD) detectors across an internal spindle at $10\text{--}20\,\text{Hz}$ to sweep a $360^\circ$ panoramic point cloud.

[^fn-laser-class1-safety]: **Laser Class 1**: The class of IEC 60825-1 whose emission is safe under all reasonably foreseeable viewing, including through optical instruments [@iec60825part1]. Below about $1{,}400\,\text{nm}$ the eye focuses the beam onto the retina, while at $1{,}550\,\text{nm}$ the cornea and lens absorb it first, so the permitted pulse energy is far higher. Those longer wavelengths need indium gallium arsenide detectors rather than silicon, which makes wavelength a range vs. cost choice made under a fixed safety ceiling. \index{Laser safety!Class 1}

Much like rolling-shutter cameras expose scanlines in sequence, a spinning mechanical LiDAR does not record an instantaneous 3D snapshot. Completing a full $360^\circ$ azimuth sweep requires $T_{\text{sweep}} = 1/f_{\text{scan}}$, corresponding to `{python} LidarSweep.t_sweep_str` on our robot's OS1-64 configured at `{python} LidarSweep.f_scan_str`. If the mobile base translates at velocity $\mathbf{v}$ and rotates at angular velocity $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ while the sensor spins, pulses fired at the start of the sweep ($\theta = 0^\circ$) and near completion ($\theta = 360^\circ$) originate from physically distinct vehicle poses. At our `{python} RollingShutterSkew.v_str` drive limit and an illustrative `{python} LidarSweep.omega_yaw_str` rad/s turn rate, the robot travels `{python} LidarSweep.dx_sweep_str` and rotates `{python} LidarSweep.dtheta_sweep_str` mrad (`{python} LidarSweep.dtheta_sweep_deg_str`°) during a single scan. Without motion correction, this sampling lag produces an apparent geometric tear where the end of the revolution meets the beginning, while shearing vertical structures across the corridor.

Restoring rigid geometric fidelity requires **continuous-time LiDAR de-skewing**\index{LiDAR!point cloud de-skewing}. The sensor hardware latches each point return $\mathbf{p}_i$ with an exact firing timestamp $t_i \in [t_{\text{start}}, t_{\text{start}} + T_{\text{sweep}}]$. A rigid pose transformation $\mathbf{T} \in \mathrm{SE}(3)$ encapsulates orientation and translation; we formalize pose composition and inversion in @sec-perception-coordinate-chain. Combining high-frequency (`{python} RollingShutterSkew.f_imu_str`) inertial data with wheel odometry allows the state estimator to compute the continuous trajectory of the vehicle body frame, $\mathbf{T}_{wb}(t_i)$. Applying the calibrated mounting extrinsic $\mathbf{T}_{bl}$ transforms coordinates from the LiDAR frame to the body frame, yielding the world-frame sensor pose $\mathbf{T}_{wl}(t_i) = \mathbf{T}_{wb}(t_i)\mathbf{T}_{bl}$. Each individual homogeneous point return is then projected back into the LiDAR's coordinate frame at the frame reference epoch $t_{\text{start}}$:
$$\mathbf{p}_i(t_{\text{start}}) = \mathbf{T}_{wl}^{-1}(t_{\text{start}}) \cdot \mathbf{T}_{wl}(t_i) \cdot \mathbf{p}_i(t_i)$$
@Fig-08-lidar-pointcloud reconstructs this continuous-time de-skewing across an 18 s driving trajectory through a city intersection: individual returns from a 64-beam spinning LiDAR are registered into a coherent orthographic map colored by return intensity times range (dark blue through magenta to orange). The crisp delineation of building facades, road striping, parked vehicles, and street trees holds only because each pulsed return was corrected using the estimated vehicle pose at its specific firing epoch $t_i$. Independently moving obstacles in the environment require separate velocity estimation and clustering.

::: {#fig-08-lidar-pointcloud fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Registered LiDAR point cloud**: Returns from a 64-beam spinning LiDAR on a moving car, registered into one map over about 18 s as a simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) estimator (@sec-memory-localization-slam) tracked the vehicle's trajectory, and shown in orthographic projection colored by return intensity times range. The sharp building edges and vehicles hold only because every return was placed with the pose at its own firing time; a single sweep is far sparser than this aggregate. (Credit: [Daniel L. Lu](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ouster_OS1-64_lidar_point_cloud_of_intersection_of_Folsom_and_Dore_St,_San_Francisco.png) / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0)." fig-alt="Dense point cloud of a city street intersection seen from above at an angle, colored from dark blue through magenta to orange, showing parked cars, road markings, building facades, and trees."}
![](images/png/fig08_real_lidar_pointcloud.png){width="100%"}
:::

Flash LiDAR architectures eliminate sweep distortion entirely by illuminating the entire field of view with a single laser pulse, capturing an instantaneous 3D range matrix. However, distributing finite optical pulse energy across a wide solid angle severely limits maximum operational range compared to concentrated, steerable beams.

Millimeter-wave radar offers an orthogonal active sensing channel, operating in the $76\text{--}81\,\text{GHz}$ band ($\lambda \approx 3.9\,\text{mm}$). Rather than emitting short, high-energy pulses, **Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar**\index{Radar!FMCW} transmits linear frequency chirps whose instantaneous carrier frequency sweeps across bandwidth $B$ over chirp duration $T_c$ with slope $S = B / T_c$. When the emitted waveform reflects from an obstacle at range $R$, the echo returns delayed by round-trip flight time $\tau = 2R/c$. Mixing the received echo with a replica of the transmitted signal generates an intermediate frequency (IF) beat tone at frequency $f_b$:
$$f_b = S \cdot \tau = \frac{2 R B}{c \, T_c}$$
Computing a fast Fourier transform across the digitized fast-time samples of each chirp (the **Range-FFT**) extracts metric range $R$ directly, without requiring optical contrast or ambient scene illumination. Physical range resolution depends strictly on total sweep bandwidth:
$$\Delta R = \frac{c}{2B}$$
For a standard `{python} ActiveSensorScales.b_chirp_str` radar sweep ($77\text{--}81\,\text{GHz}$), FMCW radar achieves a fine range resolution of $\Delta R \approx$ `{python} ActiveSensorScales.dr_radar_str`.

The transmitted chirps simultaneously encode radial velocity and bearing. A moving target shifts the phase of successive chirp reflections proportionally to its Doppler velocity; evaluating a second Fourier transform across chirps (the Doppler-FFT) extracts this radial velocity\index{Radar!Doppler velocity} within a single coherent processing interval, avoiding the latency and noise of multi-frame position differencing. Array processing across multiple receive antennas resolves target azimuth and elevation, albeit at substantially coarser angular resolution than optical LiDAR. While our mobile warehouse robot does not mount radar, millimeter-wave sensing represents a critical sensing modality for outdoor autonomous platforms. Its millimeter wavelength penetrates airborne obscurants—such as airborne dust, fog, and steam—that scatter optical wavelengths (@sec-perception-failure-modes). However, radar returns remain sensitive to specular scattering, surface orientation, and multi-path ghost targets, providing complementary evidence rather than an infallible, all-weather guarantee.

### Tactile contact grounding via optical elastomers {#sec-perception-tactile-grounding}

At the end-effector interface, external cameras and range finders cannot measure contact pressure or verify friction adhesion during physical manipulation; indeed, the gripper structure often occludes the contact patch entirely. An optical tactile sensor[^fn-gelsight-tactile-touch] addresses this perceptual blind spot by mounting a compliant, internally illuminated elastomer membrane on the fingertip and imaging its deformation with an internal camera. Photometric stereo algorithms translate surface shading into calibrated local contact topography, while tracking arrays of embedded fiducial markers yields direct measurements of tangential shear strain and incipient slip. Converting these raw optical deformations into a calibrated contact wrench requires a validated finite-element or empirical model that accounts for elastomer hysteresis, dynamic loading, and mechanical wear over time.

[^fn-gelsight-tactile-touch]: **GelSight**: Adelson's group at MIT turned a reflective elastomer skin and an internal camera into a contact sensor that recovers surface geometry and, from painted markers, shear force [@yuan2017gelsight]. The design makes touch one more image stream, so a tactile frame carries an exposure, a readout, and a calibration of its own and must be dated and qualified like the navigation camera's. \index{Tactile sensing!GelSight}

Tactile sensing thus governs the terminal contact phase of robotic grasping, whereas external cameras and range sensors guide the initial approach trajectory. Across both regimes, systems consistency demands rigorous temporal timestamps and validated geometric extrinsics. Downstream estimators cannot treat sensor outputs as abstract, timeless tensors; every tactile frame and spatial point cloud carries a finite physical age and calibration uncertainty that bound downstream safety claims.
## Dating and Placing the Measurement {#sec-perception-handoff}

A frame from the navigation camera lands in host memory as an array of pixel values. Nothing in that array says when the light was captured, where the camera was mounted, or how far a position read from it can be trusted, yet the planner that checks rack-end clearance needs all three. Every modality has the same gap: a trajectory optimizer cannot plan against unorganized time-of-flight returns, and a force controller cannot track a grid of raw intensities. Downstream estimation, planning, and spatial memory require structured physical state—metric positions, velocities, bounding volumes, and semantic classes. Translating raw streams into that state is the perception pipeline's responsibility. Whatever form its output takes, whether an explicit message packet or an observation token sequence, it must carry three mandatory properties before any consumer can use it: a capture timestamp, a reference frame, and a qualified uncertainty envelope.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_s.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Sense node."}
*The Sense stage: photons become dated, framed claims.*
:::

The first mandatory property is the **capture timestamp**\index{Capture timestamp!definition} $t_0$, which specifies the temporal midpoint of the physical energy integration window—the effective moment the camera shutter was open or the laser pulse fired. Physical sensors do not take instantaneous snapshots. An optical camera integrates photons across an exposure duration, and a mechanical lidar sweeps laser pulses over an azimuth arc across several milliseconds. Downstream state observers and vision-language-action policies require $t_0$ to ground observation tokens into the machine's dynamic equations of motion. By contrast, the arrival stamp $t_{\text{recv}}$ marks the moment the operating system kernel completes the direct memory access (DMA) transfer. Half of the exposure duration, sensor readout, physical transport, and host DMA transfer all elapse before that interrupt fires. Consequently, the arrival offset $\tau_{\text{recv}} = t_{\text{recv}} - t_0$ is never zero. Substituting arrival time for capture time directly corrupts downstream state estimation and action generation.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-arrival-stamp
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ARRIVAL-TIMESTAMP OFFSET ON THE NAVIGATION CAMERA
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The capture-timestamp paragraph of @sec-perception-handoff.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size the error an estimator makes when it dates the navigation
# │          camera's frame at DMA completion instead of at the exposure midpoint.
# │ Show:    26.6 ms from exposure midpoint to DMA completion; 39.9 mm of base
# │          travel at the 1.5 m/s drive limit.
# │ How:     t_recv - t0 = t_exp/2 + t_readout + t_transport + t_dma from
# │          RM.nav_camera and AISLE; displacement via
# │          calc_spatial_information_age_displacement.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class ArrivalStampOffset:
    """Age hidden by an arrival timestamp on the running machine's navigation camera."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    camera = RM.nav_camera  # category: datasheet (registry: navigation camera)
    t_exp = camera.exposure_time  # category: chosen (configured exposure)
    t_readout = camera.readout_time  # category: datasheet
    t_transport = AISLE.t_transport  # category: illustrative
    t_dma = AISLE.t_dma  # category: illustrative
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    tau_recv = (t_exp / 2 + t_readout + t_transport + t_dma).to(millisecond)
    dx_recv = calc_spatial_information_age_displacement(v, tau_recv).to(ureg.millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(tau_recv.magnitude - 26.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected arrival offset: {tau_recv}")
    check(abs(dx_recv.magnitude - 39.9) < 0.05, f"Unexpected arrival-stamp displacement: {dx_recv}")
    check(tau_recv < AISLE.perception_age, "Arrival offset must be part of the full observation age")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    tau_recv_str = fmt_latency(tau_recv, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    dx_recv_str = fmt_length(dx_recv, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v.to(meter / second), unit=meter / second, precision=1)
```

At constant velocity $v$, the hidden travel is $\Delta x = v\,\tau_{\text{recv}}$. On the mobile manipulator, the navigation camera's frame completes its DMA transfer `{python} ArrivalStampOffset.tau_recv_str` after the exposure midpoint. An estimator that timestamps the frame upon arrival dates the measurement late by that full duration. At the base's `{python} ArrivalStampOffset.v_str` drive limit, this temporal mismatch pairs the visual observation with an estimated pose `{python} ArrivalStampOffset.dx_recv_str` ahead of the physical position the camera occupied at capture.
