Eliminating this arrival offset and bounding the camera-to-inertial offset $\Delta t$ of @sec-perception-transduction-calibration require stamping the capture event directly in hardware rather than recording when a software thread first handles the frame buffer. Software timestamps inherit operating system scheduling jitter, driver queue delays, and thread preemption. While the base rotates at `{python} RollingShutterSkew.omega_yaw_str` rad/s, each millisecond of scheduling jitter misorients the camera by `{python} CaptureTimingScale.dtheta_per_ms_str`, producing a lateral displacement of `{python} CaptureTimingScale.dy_per_ms_jitter_str` at rack-end distance. Two hardware architectures eliminate this jitter. In the first architecture, a hardware GPIO strobe (such as FSYNC) from the IMU microcontroller simultaneously latches an inertial sample and triggers the camera exposure. Because this trigger edge marks only the start of exposure for the first sensor row rather than the optical midpoint, the driver must add $t_{\text{exp}}/2$ to reach the exposure midpoint, plus $y\,t_{\text{row}}$ for the specific image row $y$ under consideration. Omitting this correction dates the navigation camera frame `{python} CaptureTimingScale.t_trigger_corr_str` early, translating to `{python} CaptureTimingScale.dx_trigger_str` of unmodeled travel at the drive limit. Furthermore, because automatic exposure control varies $t_{\text{exp}}$ dynamically across frames, the driver must apply the specific exposure time reported in each frame's metadata. In the second architecture, used for networked sensors such as the lidar units and GigE Vision cameras, each peripheral timestamps samples against an onboard hardware clock. The Precision Time Protocol (PTP) [@ieee15882019], or its time-sensitive networking profile gPTP [@ieee8021as2020], disciplines these local clocks to a master reference across the Ethernet bus. @Sec-perception-qualifying-error details how to measure and bound the resulting clock synchronization error.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ @Sec-memory-reference-frames adds how these sensor-to-body transforms go stale over time.
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-extrinsic-error
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ EXTRINSIC ANGLE ERRORS AGAINST THE AISLE'S CLEARANCES
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The reference-frame paragraph of @sec-perception-handoff, the
# │          transform-chain paragraph of @sec-perception-error-clearance, and
# │          the calibration takeaway.
# │
# │ Goal:    Tie two lever-arm errors to the stopping budget's terms: an
# │          uncalibrated 1 degree mount error at 15 m against the base's side
# │          clearance, and a 0.005 rad extrinsic shift at 10 m against delta_loc.
# │ Show:    0.26 m, about 1.7x the 0.15 m side clearance; 50 mm, the whole
# │          delta_loc allowance.
# │ How:     Delta_y = d sin(theta); delta_x = z theta; AISLE.side_clearance and
# │          AISLE.delta_loc.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_multiple, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class ExtrinsicErrorBudget:
    """Lever-arm errors from angular mount errors, set against the aisle clearances."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    theta_frame = 1.0 * ureg.degree  # category: illustrative (uncalibrated mount error)
    d_frame = 15.0 * meter  # category: illustrative (detection range)
    theta_ext = 0.005 * radian  # category: illustrative (extrinsic shift after shock)
    z_ext = 10.0 * meter  # category: illustrative (target range)
    side_clearance = AISLE.side_clearance  # category: illustrative
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    dy_frame = (d_frame * math.sin(theta_frame.to(radian).magnitude)).to(meter)
    dy_over_side = (dy_frame / side_clearance).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    dx_ext = (z_ext * theta_ext.magnitude).to(ureg.millimeter)
    dx_over_loc = (dx_ext / delta_loc).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(dy_frame.magnitude - 0.2618) < 0.0005, f"Unexpected 1-degree lever-arm error: {dy_frame}")
    check(dy_frame > side_clearance, "Prose says the 1-degree error exceeds the side clearance")
    check(abs(dx_ext.magnitude - 50.0) < 0.05, f"Unexpected extrinsic-shift error: {dx_ext}")
    check(abs(dx_over_loc - 1.0) < 1e-9, "Prose says the extrinsic shift spends all of delta_loc")
    # margin_clearance_slip_ladder.svg fig-alt hand-types 262 mm, 50 mm and 150 mm.
    check(round(dy_frame.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude) == 262, f"Slip-ladder mount rung drifted: {dy_frame}")
    check(
        abs(delta_loc.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9 and abs(side_clearance.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude - 150.0) < 1e-9,
        "Slip-ladder reference lines drifted",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    theta_frame_str = fmt(theta_frame.to(ureg.degree).magnitude, precision=0)
    d_frame_str = fmt_length(d_frame, unit=meter, precision=0)
    dy_frame_str = fmt_length(dy_frame, unit=meter, precision=2)
    dy_over_side_mult_str = fmt_multiple(dy_over_side, precision=1)
    side_clearance_str = fmt_length(side_clearance.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    theta_ext_str = fmt(theta_ext.magnitude, precision=3)
    z_ext_str = fmt_length(z_ext, unit=meter, precision=0)
    dx_ext_str = fmt_length(dx_ext, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(delta_loc.to(ureg.millimeter), unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
```

The second mandatory property is the **reference frame**\index{Reference frame!definition} identifier $\mathcal{F}_{\text{sensor}}$. Every spatial measurement is natively resolved in the local coordinate system of the physical transducer: a camera measures bearing angles relative to its optical center, whereas a radar measures range and Doppler velocity relative to its antenna array. Downstream trajectory planners and occupancy maps, by contrast, operate in a chassis body frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{body}}$ or an inertial navigation frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{world}}$. Transforming an observation from $\mathcal{F}_{\text{sensor}}$ to $\mathcal{F}_{\text{body}}$ requires applying a rigid-body spatial transformation consisting of a rotation matrix and a translation vector that define the sensor mounting extrinsics—the calibrated physical location and orientation where the sensor is bolted onto the machine. Coordinate frames nest hierarchically from the physical operating environment down to the transducer: $\mathcal{F}_{\text{earth}} \to \mathcal{F}_{\text{map}} \to \mathcal{F}_{\text{odom}} \to \mathcal{F}_{\text{body}} \to \mathcal{F}_{\text{sensor}}$, where every link in this tree introduces its own transform and uncertainty, as diagrammed in @fig-08-coordinate-frame-tree.

When perception outputs omit the frame identifier or rely on nominal CAD dimensions rather than calibrated physical extrinsics, small angular offsets create large spatial errors that scale with distance. For example, an uncalibrated pitch or yaw error of $\theta =$ `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.theta_frame_str`° on a sensor detecting an object at range $d =$ `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.d_frame_str` induces a transverse position error $\Delta y \approx d \sin\theta$ of `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.dy_frame_str`. This lateral offset is approximately `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.dy_over_side_mult_str` the `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.side_clearance_str` side clearance that the base maintains from the warehouse racks, causing the planner to either steer into the racking or falsely reject an open aisle as obstructed.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_clearance_slip_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Five horizontal bars in millimeters, longest at top: 1 degree mount 262 millimeters, full age 77.4, arrival stamp 39.9, row skew 24.9, trigger stamp 12 millimeters. A dotted slate line marks the 50 millimeter localization allowance and a dashed red line marks the 150 millimeter side clearance; only the mount bar crosses the red line."}

*Timing slips cost tens of millimeters; a `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.theta_frame_str`° mount error costs `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.dy_frame_str`.*
:::

The third mandatory property is an **uncertainty representation**\index{Uncertainty envelope!definition}, such as a measurement covariance $\mathbf{\Sigma}_z$ paired with a validated tail bound or hard error envelope when physical clearance depends on it. Environmental degradations such as low illumination, atmospheric scattering, specular reflections, and out-of-distribution neural network errors distort the residual distribution far beyond Gaussian assumptions. While a covariance matrix characterizes second moments, it does not guarantee a conservative bounding volume for the true physical state. Downstream state estimators and policy heads rely on $\mathbf{\Sigma}_z$ to weight incoming sensory updates against dynamic motion predictions. If perception reports an artificially optimistic covariance, the estimator over-weights spurious measurements and commands aggressive, erratic actuator responses. Robust physical safety decisions must therefore account explicitly for systematic bias, missed detections, and sensor operational limits alongside the reported covariance.

### Calibrating the coordinate chain {#sec-perception-coordinate-chain}

A coordinate frame transform maps a point expressed relative to one origin into the coordinate system of another. Its rotational component reorients the coordinate axes, while its translational component accounts for the spatial displacement between origins. Homogeneous matrix representations package these operations so that camera-to-wrist, wrist-to-base, and base-to-world relationships can be composed at the exact capture instant $t_0$. The engineering requirement is that every link in the kinematic chain describe the true physical mounting and instantaneous pose at that capture time.

A robot's spatial coordinate system forms a **directed acyclic graph (DAG)** of transforms $\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})$, where vertices $\mathcal{V} = \{\mathcal{F}_i\}$ represent physical coordinate frames and directed edges $\mathcal{E}$ represent time-varying rigid-body transforms $\mathbf{T}_{ij}(t) \in \text{SE}(3)$. In practice, systems constrain this DAG to a directed tree where each non-root frame has exactly one parent, ensuring a unique path between any two frames. When unprojecting an optical observation $\mathbf{p}_{\text{cam}}(t_0)$ into world coordinates, the runtime composes the transforms along that tree:
$$\mathbf{p}_{\text{world}}(t_0) = \mathbf{T}_{\text{world}}^{\text{map}} \cdot \mathbf{T}_{\text{map}}^{\text{odom}}(t_0) \cdot \mathbf{T}_{\text{odom}}^{\text{base}}(t_0) \cdot \mathbf{T}_{\text{base}}^{\text{flange}}(t_0) \cdot \mathbf{T}_{\text{flange}}^{\text{cam}} \cdot \mathbf{p}_{\text{cam}}(t_0)$$
The physical mounting location of the sensor on the kinematic chain dictates how coordinate transforms update across this DAG:

In an **eye-in-hand**\index{Eye-in-hand calibration!definition} configuration, the camera or depth sensor is bolted directly to the manipulator's moving tool flange ($\mathcal{F}_{\text{flange}}$). Moving any preceding joint alters the sensor's optical center relative to the world, requiring continuous forward kinematics updates. Solving for the rigid extrinsic transform $\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{T}_{\text{flange}}^{\text{cam}} \in \text{SE}(3)$ requires executing robot motions across $N \ge 2$ non-parallel rotational axes while observing a stationary fiducial target, such as a ChArUco grid.[^fn-charuco-calibration-board] For two distinct poses $k$ and $k+1$, the closed kinematic loop establishes the classic **hand-eye matrix equation**:[^fn-handeye-calibration-origin]
$$\mathbf{A} \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{X} \mathbf{B}$$
where $\mathbf{A} = (\mathbf{T}_{\text{base}, k}^{\text{flange}})^{-1} \mathbf{T}_{\text{base}, k+1}^{\text{flange}} \in \text{SE}(3)$ is the relative flange displacement reported by the forward kinematics chain, and $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{T}_{\text{cam}, k}^{\text{target}} (\mathbf{T}_{\text{cam}, k+1}^{\text{target}})^{-1} \in \text{SE}(3)$ is the relative camera displacement extracted from optical target unprojection.

[^fn-charuco-calibration-board]: **ChArUco Board**: A chessboard whose white squares carry uniquely coded ArUco markers. The chessboard corners give subpixel accuracy and the codes identify which corners are in view, so calibration works from partial views of the board, the usual case for a camera on a moving wrist. \index{Calibration!ChArUco target}

[^fn-handeye-calibration-origin]: **Hand-Eye Calibration**: The problem was posed as $\mathbf{AX}=\mathbf{XB}$ independently by @shiu1989calibration and @tsai1989new, for cameras bolted to robot wrists. The camera's pose relative to the flange is never measured directly, only inferred from paired motions, so any error in $\mathbf{X}$ enters every grasp the arm plans from that camera, and poorly spread calibration motions leave it weakly determined. \index{Calibration!hand-eye}

In an **eye-to-hand**\index{Eye-to-hand calibration!definition} calibration rig, the camera overlooks the workspace from a body-mounted mast or a stationary overhead beam. When calibrating against an overhead camera, the mobile base must remain parked so that the camera-to-base transform remains constant ($\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{T}_{\text{base}}^{\text{cam}} \in \text{SE}(3)$), while the target is affixed to the robot's moving end-effector ($\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{T}_{\text{flange}}^{\text{target}} \in \text{SE}(3)$). At each joint configuration, let $\mathbf{A} = (\mathbf{T}_{\text{base}}^{\text{flange}})^{-1}$ map base coordinates into the flange frame and $\mathbf{B} = (\mathbf{T}_{\text{cam}}^{\text{target}})^{-1}$ map camera coordinates into the target frame. These are absolute pose transforms for this rig, rather than the relative motions used above. Both paths then map camera coordinates into the flange frame:
$$\mathbf{A} \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{Z} \mathbf{B}$$
If the mobile base subsequently moves relative to the overhead camera, the runtime must update the camera-to-base transform accordingly.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-link-thermal-expansion
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THERMAL EXPANSION OF AN ALUMINUM LINK
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The calibration-drift paragraph of @sec-perception-coordinate-chain.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size the length change of a warmed aluminum link.
# │ Show:    23e-6/K x 1 m x 10 K = 0.23 mm.
# │ How:     dL = alpha * L * dT.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, check

class LinkThermalExpansion:
    """Length change of a uniformly warmed aluminum link."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    alpha = 23e-6 / ureg.kelvin  # category: illustrative (typical structural aluminum; alloy datasheet supplies the exact value)
    l_link = 1.0 * meter  # category: illustrative (link length)
    d_temp = 10.0 * ureg.kelvin  # category: illustrative (uniform warming)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    dl = (alpha * l_link * d_temp).to(ureg.millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(dl.magnitude - 0.23) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected expansion: {dl}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    alpha_str = fmt(alpha.to(1 / ureg.kelvin).magnitude * 1e6, precision=0)
    l_link_str = fmt_length(l_link, unit=meter, precision=0)
    d_temp_str = fmt(d_temp.to(ureg.kelvin).magnitude, precision=0)
    dl_str = fmt_length(dl, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
```

Treating the nominal rigid transform chain from CAD as an exact physical calibration ignores load and temperature effects. Physical manipulators exhibit mechanical compliance under payload mass, lost motion and torsional wind-up in the joints (strain wave gears have near-zero backlash, but their flexsplines still twist under load), and thermal expansion (structural aluminum expands at $\alpha \approx$ `{python} LinkThermalExpansion.alpha_str`$\times 10^{-6}/\text{K}$). For an illustrative `{python} LinkThermalExpansion.l_link_str` aluminum link that warms uniformly by `{python} LinkThermalExpansion.d_temp_str`$^\circ\text{C}$, the corresponding expansion is `{python} LinkThermalExpansion.dl_str`. A motor temperature rise alone does not establish that link-temperature change, as localized thermal gradients across structural members and encoder mountings require direct measurement before updating calibration parameters.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-wrist-timestamp-skew
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ JOINT-TO-CAMERA TIMESTAMP SKEW AT THE WRIST
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The joint-kinematics timing paragraph of
# │          @sec-perception-coordinate-chain.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size the wrist-camera error from a joint/camera timestamp skew and
# │          the largest skew a grasp tolerance allows.
# │ Show:    10 mm + 3 mm = 13 mm for a 10 ms skew; 3.8 ms allowed for 5 mm.
# │ How:     dp = (v + omega r) dt; dt_max = eps_pos / (v + omega r).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check

class WristTimestampSkew:
    """Wrist-camera position error from joint/camera timestamp skew."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v_wrist = 1.0 * meter / second  # category: illustrative (wrist linear speed)
    omega_wrist = 2.0 * radian / second  # category: illustrative (wrist angular speed)
    r_cam = 0.15 * meter  # category: illustrative (camera lever arm)
    dt_skew = 10.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (unmodeled skew)
    eps_pos = 5.0 * ureg.millimeter  # category: illustrative (grasp position tolerance)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_eff = (v_wrist + omega_wrist.to(1 / second).magnitude * r_cam / second).to(meter / second)
    dp_lin = (v_wrist * dt_skew).to(ureg.millimeter)
    dp_rot = ((v_eff - v_wrist) * dt_skew).to(ureg.millimeter)
    dp = (dp_lin + dp_rot).to(ureg.millimeter)
    dt_max = (eps_pos / v_eff).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(dp.magnitude - 13.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected skew error: {dp}")
    check(abs(dt_max.magnitude - 3.85) < 0.01, f"Unexpected skew bound: {dt_max}")
    check(dt_max > 1.0 * millisecond, "Prose says millisecond-level alignment suffices")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    v_wrist_str = fmt_velocity(v_wrist, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    omega_wrist_str = fmt(omega_wrist.to(radian / second).magnitude, precision=0)
    r_cam_str = fmt_length(r_cam, unit=meter, precision=2)
    dt_skew_str = fmt_latency(dt_skew, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    dp_lin_str = fmt_length(dp_lin, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    dp_rot_str = fmt_length(dp_rot, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    dp_str = fmt_length(dp, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    eps_pos_str = fmt_length(eps_pos, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    dt_max_str = fmt_latency(dt_max, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

Fusing joint kinematics with optical frames also requires temporal alignment across the transform DAG. Any uncalibrated timestamp skew $dt = t_{\text{cam}} - t_{\text{joint}}$ between the motor communication bus (such as EtherCAT or CANopen) and the camera exposure window evaluates the forward kinematics chain at stale joint angles $\mathbf{q}(t_{\text{joint}}) \neq \mathbf{q}(t_{\text{cam}})$, inducing spatial tracking error:
$$\Delta \mathbf{p}_{\text{skew}} = \mathbf{v}_{\text{wrist}} \, dt + (\boldsymbol{\omega}_{\text{wrist}} \times \mathbf{r}_{\text{cam}}) \, dt$$
At an illustrative wrist linear velocity $v =$ `{python} WristTimestampSkew.v_wrist_str` and angular velocity $\omega =$ `{python} WristTimestampSkew.omega_wrist_str` rad/s with a camera lever arm $r =$ `{python} WristTimestampSkew.r_cam_str`, an unmodeled `{python} WristTimestampSkew.dt_skew_str` skew displaces the observation by `{python} WristTimestampSkew.dp_lin_str` plus `{python} WristTimestampSkew.dp_rot_str`, or `{python} WristTimestampSkew.dp_str`. This error causes the arm to miss a grasp whose position tolerance is `{python} WristTimestampSkew.eps_pos_str`. The timing requirement follows directly from that tolerance: the skew must satisfy $dt \le \epsilon_{\text{pos}}/(v + \omega r)$, which evaluates to `{python} WristTimestampSkew.dt_max_str`. Millisecond-level alignment therefore suffices, whereas microsecond synchronization is unnecessary. Systems typically meet this requirement by timestamping both streams against a single shared clock—such as a fieldbus distributed clock or a PTP master—and interpolating the high-rate joint stream at the camera's exposure midpoint.

The [REP 105 frame convention](https://reps.openrobotics.org/rep-0105/)\index{Standards!REP 105}[^fn-rep-ros-conventions] names these frames and separates a locally continuous `odom` pose from a globally corrected `map` pose. On the mobile manipulator, $\mathcal{F}_{\text{body}}$ is the base's `base_link`, tracked through the odometric frame `odom`, and the arm's serial chain maps its mounting flange `tool0` through the joint angles back to `base_link`. @Tbl-08-rep105-tree lists the frame roles and the behavioral rules each consumer follows. A local controller consumes a continuous estimate and rejects unexpected transform jumps, while runtime checks verify transform timestamps and estimator uncertainties before execution.

[^fn-rep-ros-conventions]: **ROS Enhancement Proposal (REP)**: The Robot Operating System records its community conventions as numbered REPs, a process copied from Python's enhancement proposals. REP 105 fixes the meaning of `map`, `odom`, and `base_link` and the continuity each must keep [@meeussen2010rep105], so a frame name written into a record denotes the same physical frame for every consumer that reads it. \index{Standards!ROS Enhancement Proposal}

| Frame         | Parent in this example | Meaning                                     | Consumer rule                                                 |
|:--------------|:-----------------------|:--------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|
| `earth`       | root                   | Optional geodetic datum                     | Verify datum before global routing                            |
| `map`         | `earth` if present     | Global localization; corrections may jump   | Keep relocalization jumps out of local feedback               |
| `odom`        | `map`                  | Locally continuous pose estimate; may drift | Track motion locally; monitor uncertainty and discontinuities |
| `base_link`   | `odom`                 | Body-fixed origin                           | Body pose still inherits odometry uncertainty                 |
| `sensor_link` | `base_link`            | Calibrated sensor mounting frame            | Apply time-valid extrinsics and their uncertainty             |

: **REP 105 frame roles for a mobile robot**: A compact example of global, local, body, and sensor frames. REP 105 requires `odom`-relative pose to remain continuous but does not prescribe $C^1$ smoothness, a covariance growth rate, or fixed accuracy; these require estimator-specific evidence. {#tbl-08-rep105-tree tbl-colwidths="[14,20,32,34]"}

::: {#fig-08-coordinate-frame-tree fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Coordinate frame tree and its consumers**: Each edge states the property REP 105 or calibration gives it and the uncertainty it adds to the prose equation below. Only the odom to base_link edge is required to stay continuous; the map to odom correction may jump at relocalization, so local tracking loops consume the continuous branch while global planners reconcile the jump. A sensor observation reaches the consumers with its frame, capture epoch $t_0$, and covariance $\mathbf{\Sigma}_z$." fig-alt="Vertical tree of five labeled frame boxes linked by downward arrows: earth, drawn dashed as optional, then map, odom, base_link, and sensor_link. Each arrow carries a short label: fixed datum if present; may jump at relocalization with sigma map; continuous per REP 105 and drifts with sigma odom; rigid and calibrated with sigma ext. Brackets on the right group map as used by the global planner, odom and base_link as used by local tracking loops, and sensor_link as the observation carrying frame, epoch, and covariance."}
![](images/svg/fig08_coordinate_frame_tree.svg){width="90%"}
:::

@Fig-08-coordinate-frame-tree diagrams this hierarchical frame tree and its downstream consumers across five vertical tiers ($\mathcal{F}_{\text{earth}} \to \mathcal{F}_{\text{map}} \to \mathcal{F}_{\text{odom}} \to \mathcal{F}_{\text{base\_link}} \to \mathcal{F}_{\text{sensor\_link}}$): right-hand brackets decouple consumers so that global planners absorb discontinuous $\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{map}}$ jumps during relocalization, while high-rate local tracking loops consume the strictly continuous `odom` $\to$ `base_link` branch. This architectural decoupling prevents a global localization correction from manifesting as an abrupt local tracking step on physical actuators. Mounting uncertainty compounds with dynamic pose uncertainty across every intermediate link. Under a first-order propagation model with independent error sources:
$$\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{world}} = \mathbf{J}_{\text{map}}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{map}}\mathbf{J}_{\text{map}}^\top + \mathbf{J}_{\text{odom}}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{odom}}\mathbf{J}_{\text{odom}}^\top + \mathbf{J}_{\text{ext}}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{ext}}\mathbf{J}_{\text{ext}}^\top$$
where the Jacobians $\mathbf{J}$ project each frame's spatial covariance into world coordinates. When frame errors correlate, the propagation must include their cross-covariance terms. A downstream consumer requires the frame identifier, capture epoch, and compounded uncertainty envelope, rather than a transform selected merely by its latest publication timestamp.

::: {#psp-perception-observation-invariants .callout-perspective title="The three invariants of observation"}
Pass a perception claim with its capture time and clock domain, coordinate frame, and qualified uncertainty. Refuse a claim when any of those cannot be checked for the proposed motion.
:::

While capture timestamping and kinematic calibration establish the physical instant and spatial reference frame of a measurement, delivering that measurement across an embodied runtime introduces variable computational delay. Managing this latency requires constructing an explicit age budget that tracks the observation from physical energy integration through neural inference and dispatch, bounding the total information age before downstream actuators act.
## Bounding Observation Age {#sec-perception-age-budget}

Even when a rack-end observation is geometrically calibrated, the data it contains describes the past. Any delivery deadline for perception must therefore account for the full physical interval since photon capture—including hardware acquisition, transport, and queueing stages that standard neural inference benchmarks ignore.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Transduction freshness and sensor measurement aging are derived in @sec-body-measurement-freshness.
:::

::: {#dfn-perception-spatial-information-age .callout-definition title="Spatial information age"}

***Spatial information age***\index{Spatial information age!definition}\index{Information age!definition} ($t_{\text{age}}$) is the physical time elapsed between the exposure midpoint at the transducer and the consumption of the resulting observation by a policy backbone, state observer, or control loop. It is the capture-to-consumption part of the measurement age that @sec-body-measurement-freshness counts from transduction, and running text calls it observation age.

1.  **Significance**: Because the robot continues moving while the compute pipeline runs, observation age converts directly into physical displacement (@eq-percep-spatial-displacement) and expands the stopping budget through the pre-brake delay $\tau_{\text{delay}}$. On the warehouse mobile manipulator, the navigation-camera observation is already `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.t_age_str` old at dispatch—representing `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.dx_str` of blind travel at the `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.v_str` drive limit—before any downstream consumer has inspected the frame.
2.  **Distinction**: Conventional benchmark latency measures only the software execution time of a forward pass. In contrast, observation age spans the entire physical journey from photon arrival to action: the exposure midpoint, sensor rolling readout, serialized bus transport, direct memory access (DMA) transfers, driver queueing, image signal processor (ISP) conversions, model inference, inter-process dispatch, and any scheduling delay before the consumer acts on the data.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Systems engineers frequently confuse a frame's arrival timestamp in userspace memory ($t_{\text{recv}}$) with its actual physical observation time ($t_0$). On the navigation camera, the arrival timestamp overlooks `{python} ArrivalStampOffset.tau_recv_str` of front-end exposure, readout, and transport. At the maximum drive limit, this unmeasured interval conceals `{python} ArrivalStampOffset.dx_recv_str` of physical travel, saddling downstream controllers with an unmodeled phase lag.

:::

When evaluated along the machine's trajectory, observation age integrates directly into spatial displacement (@eq-percep-spatial-displacement):
$$\Delta \mathbf{x} = \int_{t_0}^{t_0+t_{\text{age}}} \mathbf{v}(t)\,dt$$ {#eq-percep-spatial-displacement}
To assess spatial uncertainty across the perception pipeline, we can combine this motion-induced displacement with first-order stereo triangulation noise and small-angle extrinsic calibration errors (@eq-percep-unified-uncertainty-envelope):
$$\epsilon_{\text{scale}} = \underbrace{\int_{t_0}^{t_0+t_{\text{age}}} \|\mathbf{v}(t)\|\,dt}_{\text{path-length travel}} + \underbrace{\frac{z^2}{fb}\sigma_d}_{\text{stereo depth standard deviation}} + \underbrace{z |\theta_{\text{ext}}|}_{\text{small-angle mounting error scale}}$$ {#eq-percep-unified-uncertainty-envelope}
The first term integrates instantaneous speed to compute path length, providing an upper bound on net translation during the perception delay. The second term characterizes depth uncertainty for a calibrated stereo camera with baseline $b$, focal length $f$, operating range $z$, and disparity standard deviation $\sigma_d$; this term represents a statistical standard-deviation scale rather than an absolute bound. The third term models the lever-arm displacement produced by a small extrinsic angular misalignment $\theta_{\text{ext}}$ over target distance $z$. Combining these terms produces an illustrative scalar error scale rather than a certified safety envelope. Guaranteeing collision clearance requires accounting for spatial vector directions, compensating systematic calibration bias, and bounding the heavy tails of empirical sensor residuals (@sec-perception-error-clearance).

### The latency waterfall {#sec-perception-latency-waterfall}

To quantify age in a representative vision pipeline, we trace the cumulative delay from the exposure midpoint to the moment the perception subsystem publishes its processed state estimate. This capture-to-dispatch interval forms the core of the perception pipeline's **observation age** ($t_{\text{age}}$)\index{Observation age!definition}. When hardware stages execute sequentially, the total age expands as a **latency waterfall**\index{Latency waterfall}; if adjacent stages overlap in hardware or stream through pipelined ring buffers, their combined duration replaces the naive sum of individual stage times:
$$t_{\text{age}} = \frac{t_{\text{exp}}}{2} + t_{\text{readout}} + t_{\text{transport}} + t_{\text{DMA}} + t_{\text{ISP}} + t_{\text{backbone}} + t_{\text{IPC}}$$ {#eq-percep-latency-waterfall}

Because a physical robot possesses mechanical momentum, observation age is not an abstract scheduling metric. It translates directly into blind physical displacement:
$$\Delta x_{\text{blind}} = v \cdot t_{\text{age}}$$
While the perception subsystem captures photons, clocks out pixel lines, transfers buffers over the bus, and executes deep neural network kernels, the chassis continues hurtling through the workspace at velocity $v$. Complete safety margins must account not only for perception latency, but also for downstream execution overheads: authorization lease expiration, control scheduler quantization ticks, fieldbus transmission times, and physical brake actuation latency. Summing these terms yields the total pre-brake delay $\tau_{\text{delay}} = t_{\text{age}} + T_{\text{lease}} + T_{\text{tick}} + T_{\text{bus}} + T_{\text{act}}$, which governs the total blind travel:
$$d_{\text{blind}} = v \cdot \tau_{\text{delay}}$$
At constant operating velocity, every millisecond of unmodeled latency drains physical clearance linearly. If an independent safety monitor or hardware permission path operates concurrently, the safety calculation must reflect that dedicated architecture rather than assuming that every stalled neural forward pass postpones emergency braking. Notebook \ref{nbk-perception-sensor-transduction-latency-spatial-information-age} steps through each hardware and software stage of this waterfall for the warehouse mobile manipulator, converting elapsed time into traveled distance.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-sensor-information-age
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ NAVIGATION-CAMERA INFORMATION AGE AND STOPPING-BUDGET ROW 5
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: \ref{nbk-perception-sensor-transduction-latency-spatial-information-age},
# │          @tbl-08-latency-budget, and the stopping-budget paragraph of
# │          @sec-perception-transduction-calibration.
# │
# │ Goal:    Sum the warehouse mobile manipulator's navigation-camera latency
# │          waterfall into t_age and add its term to the stopping budget.
# │ Show:    Stage increments and cumulative ages; t_age 51.6 ms; tau_delay
# │          133.6 ms; row 5 v*t_age 77.4 mm at 1.5 m/s; running total
# │          835.5 mm -> 912.9 mm; 187.1 mm of the 1.10 m clear distance left.
# │ How:     Stage terms from RM.nav_camera and AISLE; totals from
# │          calc_safe_stopping_distance with the Body and Nervous System terms
# │          (a_brake, delta_loc, delta_margin, lease path, brake onset). The C2
# │          suffix and tracking inset join later rows, not this one.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_time,
    fmt_display_math,
    check,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class SensorInformationAge:
    """Navigation-camera latency waterfall, t_age, and the observation-age row of the stopping budget."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    camera = RM.nav_camera  # category: datasheet (registry: Sony IMX477 navigation camera)
    t_exp = camera.exposure_time.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen (configured exposure)
    t_readout = camera.readout_time.to(millisecond)  # category: datasheet
    t_transport = AISLE.t_transport.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative
    t_dma = AISLE.t_dma.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative
    t_isp = AISLE.t_isp.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative
    t_backbone = AISLE.t_backbone.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative
    t_ipc = AISLE.t_ipc.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative
    t_act = AISLE.t_brake_onset.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative
    v = RM.base.max_velocity.to(meter / second)  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative
    delta_margin = AISLE.delta_margin  # category: chosen
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    f_frame = camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_exp_half = (t_exp / 2).to(millisecond)
    t_frame = (1 / f_frame).to(millisecond)
    age_after_exposure = t_exp_half
    age_after_readout = age_after_exposure + t_readout
    age_after_transport = age_after_readout + t_transport
    age_after_dma = age_after_transport + t_dma
    age_after_isp = age_after_dma + t_isp
    age_after_backbone = age_after_isp + t_backbone
    tau_age = (age_after_backbone + t_ipc).to(millisecond)

    tau_delay = (tau_age + t_lease + t_tick + t_bus + t_act).to(millisecond)
    dx = calc_spatial_information_age_displacement(v, tau_age).to(ureg.millimeter)
    row_age = dx
    total_before = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v, t_lease + t_tick + t_bus + t_act, a_brake, delta_loc, delta_margin).to(ureg.millimeter)
    total_after = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v, tau_delay, a_brake, delta_loc, delta_margin).to(ureg.millimeter)
    remaining = (d_clear - total_after).to(ureg.millimeter)
    dx_frame = (v * t_frame).to(ureg.millimeter)  # checkpoint: one dropped frame of extra age
    frame_share = (dx_frame / remaining).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(tau_age.magnitude - AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, f"Waterfall disagrees with AISLE.perception_age: {tau_age}")
    check(abs(tau_age.magnitude - 51.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected t_age: {tau_age}")
    check(abs(tau_delay.magnitude - AISLE.tau_delay.to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, f"Delay sum disagrees with AISLE.tau_delay: {tau_delay}")
    check(abs(tau_delay.magnitude - 133.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected tau_delay: {tau_delay}")
    check(abs(v.magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected drive limit: {v}")
    check(abs(row_age.magnitude - 77.4) < 0.05, f"Unexpected observation-age row: {row_age}")
    check(abs(total_before.magnitude - 835.5) < 0.05, f"Unexpected running total before row 5: {total_before}")
    check(abs(total_after.magnitude - 912.9) < 0.05, f"Unexpected running total after row 5: {total_after}")
    check(abs((total_after - total_before - row_age).magnitude) < 1e-6, "Row 5 does not close the running total")
    check(abs(remaining.magnitude - 187.1) < 0.05, f"Unexpected remaining clear distance: {remaining}")
    check(abs(dx_frame.magnitude - 25.0) < 0.05 and 0.13 < frame_share < 0.14, f"Checkpoint answer drifted: {dx_frame}, {frame_share}")
    check(
        t_backbone == max(t_exp_half, t_readout, t_transport, t_dma, t_isp, t_backbone, t_ipc),
        "Notebook says the backbone is the largest single stage",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_exp_str = fmt_latency(t_exp, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_exp_half_str = fmt_latency(t_exp_half, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_readout_str = fmt_latency(t_readout, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_transport_str = fmt_latency(t_transport, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_dma_str = fmt_latency(t_dma, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_isp_str = fmt_latency(t_isp, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_backbone_str = fmt_latency(t_backbone, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_ipc_str = fmt_latency(t_ipc, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    tau_age_str = fmt_latency(tau_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    tau_age_s_str = fmt_time(tau_age.to(second), 'second', precision=4)
    age_after_exposure_str = fmt_latency(age_after_exposure, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    age_after_readout_str = fmt_latency(age_after_readout, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    age_after_transport_str = fmt_latency(age_after_transport, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    age_after_dma_str = fmt_latency(age_after_dma, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    age_after_isp_str = fmt_latency(age_after_isp, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    age_after_backbone_str = fmt_latency(age_after_backbone, unit=millisecond, precision=1)

    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_bus_str = fmt_latency(t_bus, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_act_str = fmt_latency(t_act, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    tau_delay_str = fmt_latency(tau_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)

    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    dx_m_str = fmt_length(dx.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=4)
    dx_mm_str = fmt_length(dx, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    row_age_str = fmt_length(row_age, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    total_before_str = fmt_length(total_before, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    total_after_str = fmt_length(total_after, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    remaining_str = fmt_length(remaining, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    t_frame_str = fmt_latency(t_frame, unit=millisecond, precision=1)

    tau_age_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"t_{{\text{{age}}}} = {t_exp_half_str} + {t_readout_str} + {t_transport_str} + {t_dma_str} + {t_isp_str} + {t_backbone_str} + {t_ipc_str} = {tau_age_str}"
    )
    dx_display_math = fmt_display_math(rf"\Delta x = ({v_str}) \times ({tau_age_s_str}) = {dx_m_str} = {dx_mm_str}")
    t_rest_str = fmt_latency((t_lease + t_tick + t_bus + t_act).to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    tau_delay_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\tau_{{\text{{delay}}}} = \underbrace{{t_{{\text{{age}}}}}}_{{{tau_age_str}}} + \underbrace{{T_{{\text{{lease}}}} + T_{{\text{{tick}}}} + T_{{\text{{bus}}}} + T_{{\text{{act}}}}}}_{{{t_rest_str}}} = {tau_delay_str}"
    )
    d_stop_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"d_{{\text{{stop}}}} = \underbrace{{d_{{\text{{base}}}} + d_{{\text{{lease}}}}}}_{{{total_before_str}}} + \underbrace{{v \cdot t_{{\text{{age}}}}}}_{{{row_age_str}}} = {total_after_str}"
    )
```

::: {#nbk-perception-sensor-transduction-latency-spatial-information-age .callout-notebook title="Travel before the frame is read"}

**Problem**: The mobile manipulator drives toward a rack end at its drive limit when a person steps out. How old is the navigation camera's observation of that person when perception dispatches it, and how far has the base traveled by then?

**Variables**:

* Exposure $t_{\text{exp}} =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_exp_str` (Chosen low-light setting), so the midpoint lag is $t_{\text{exp}}/2 =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_exp_half_str`; rolling readout $t_{\text{readout}} =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_readout_str` (Datasheet).
* Residual MIPI CSI-2 transport $t_{\text{transport}} =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_transport_str` (Illustrative). The [Sony IMX477 flyer](https://www.sony-semicon.com/files/62/pdf/p-13_IMX477-AACK_Flyer.pdf) specifies a four-lane option up to $2.1\text{ Gbps/lane}$; the budget assigns only the transport left after streaming readout, not frame size divided by peak lane rate.
* DMA and driver queue $t_{\text{DMA}} =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_dma_str`, ISP debayering and rectification $t_{\text{ISP}} =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_isp_str`, INT8 vision backbone $t_{\text{backbone}} =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_backbone_str`, and covariance packaging with zero-copy dispatch $t_{\text{IPC}} =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_ipc_str` (all Illustrative).
* Drive limit $v =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.v_str` (Illustrative).

**Math**:

*Age at dispatch.* The serial stages of @eq-percep-latency-waterfall sum to
`{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_display_math`

*Travel.* Holding speed through the age window:
`{python} SensorInformationAge.dx_display_math`

*Sensitivity.* Each further millisecond in any stage adds `{python} CaptureTimingScale.dx_per_ms_str` of travel at the drive limit.

**Result**: The observation is `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str` old at dispatch, and the base has covered `{python} SensorInformationAge.dx_mm_str`. The backbone is the largest single stage, but exposure and readout alone contribute `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_readout_str` before any computation starts.

**Systems insight**: The base covers this distance before the perception record exists. Timestamped pose propagation can place the old observation correctly in the current frame, but no later stage returns the distance already traveled, so $v\,t_{\text{age}}$ enters the stopping budget as a term of its own.

:::

The seven stages of @tbl-08-latency-budget sum to the dispatch age $t_{\text{age}} =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str`. The existing stopping ledger then adds the active lease and response path of @sec-nervous-cadences:
`{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_delay_display_math`

This subtotal forms a **partial delay ledger** rather than an end-to-end capture-to-response bound. In the timing breakdown of @tbl-04-event-ledger, perception governs the first interval from capture to dispatch, while actuator mechanics govern the third interval of physical braking. The observation continues to age across the intermediate second interval while the proposer completes inference, transmits the candidate trajectory, and awaits admission from the safety checker. Let $\Delta_{\text{da}}$ denote this dispatch-to-admission interval, encompassing model planning and inter-process communication overheads. Because an active lease takes effect only upon candidate admission, the total delay under a stalled-proposer fault equals the displayed subtotal plus $\Delta_{\text{da}}$. In @Sec-placement, \ref{nbk-placement-transport-budget} allocates a budget for $\Delta_{\text{da}}$ that awaits empirical validation on hardware. Because that allocation accounts for full inference after dispatch while the neural vision backbone is already budgeted here, their direct sum provides a conservative bound; empirical timestamping on the loaded machine is required to isolate nonoverlapping execution intervals.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ @Sec-placement-isolation-decisions allocates $\Delta_{\text{da}}$ for the discrete placement, as a budget still to be qualified.
:::

@Fig-08-capture-to-brake-strip sequences this partial delay ledger across three synchronized lanes (camera, host, and response) over an absolute millisecond timeline and paired base travel: the camera lane tracks exposure midpoint and readout; the host lane stages link transport, DMA, ISP processing, vision backbone inference, and IPC queueing up to dispatch at `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str`; and the response lane sequences execution lease expiration, control tick, bus transmission, and mechanical actuator onset reaching `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_delay_str`. A vertical dashed partition at dispatch marks where the unbounded dispatch-to-admission interval $\Delta_{\text{da}}$ inserts additional delay, shifting all downstream brake-onset events to the right.

::: {#fig-08-capture-to-brake-strip fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Capture-to-brake timing strip**: Time runs from the exposure midpoint of the frame that first shows the hazard. The camera and host lanes carry the navigation camera's serial stages, with link, DMA, and ISP drawn as one segment, to dispatch at `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str`; the response lane adds the lease, tick, bus, and actuator onset of a stalled proposer to reach `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_delay_str`. The row beneath reads the same axis as base travel at the `{python} SensorInformationAge.v_str` drive limit. The dashed line at dispatch marks where the dispatch-to-admission interval $\Delta_{\text{da}}$ enters; this chapter does not bound it, so every later event shifts right by its measured value." fig-alt="Horizontal timing strip with three lanes labeled camera, host, and response over a time axis in milliseconds. The camera lane shows a solid exposure bar centered on the capture line and a readout bar after it. The host lane shows a combined link, DMA, and ISP bar, a longer backbone bar, and a thin IPC bar ending at a dispatch line. A dashed line at dispatch is labeled as the point where unbounded dispatch-to-admission time enters. The response lane starts at dispatch with a long lease bar, a thin tick and bus bar, and an onset bar ending at a brake-onset line. A bracket over the strip spans capture to brake onset. A travel row beneath marks millimeters of base travel and the travel before and after dispatch."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-perception-capture-to-brake
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CAPTURE-TO-BRAKE TIMING STRIP (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-08-capture-to-brake-strip in @sec-perception-latency-waterfall.
# │
# │ Goal:    Put the navigation camera's dispatch age and the stalled-proposer
# │          response path on one clock, with the travel each consumes.
# │ Show:    exposure and readout; link, DMA, ISP, backbone, IPC to t_age; the
# │          point where the unbounded Delta_da enters; lease, tick, bus, and
# │          onset to tau_delay; travel at the drive limit.
# │ How:     viz.perception_age_strip (the shared timing-strip family) reads
# │          every duration from AISLE; the guards tie its drawn events to
# │          SensorInformationAge.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.fmt import check
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

SIA = SensorInformationAge

# ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
v_strip = SIA.v  # category: illustrative (drive limit)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
strip_08 = viz.perception_age_strip(AISLE, v_strip)
t_dispatch_drawn = next(e.t for e in strip_08.events if e.label.startswith("dispatch"))
t_onset_drawn = next(e.t for e in strip_08.events if e.label == "brake onset")

# ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(t_dispatch_drawn - SIA.tau_age.to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "The strip's dispatch must equal t_age.")
check(abs(t_onset_drawn - SIA.tau_delay.to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "The strip's brake onset must equal tau_delay.")
check(
    abs(strip_08.speed_mm_per_unit * t_dispatch_drawn - SIA.row_age.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-6,
    "The travel to dispatch must equal the observation-age row.",
)

# ┌── 4. PLOT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax, axd = viz.plot_timing_strip(strip_08)
plt.show()
```

:::

Because the hardware permission path validates geometric safety without reprocessing raw images, it cannot retroactively compress this perception pipeline delay; the age reaches it strictly through the proposal's stamped evidence epoch. At the `{python} SensorInformationAge.v_str` drive limit, the observation-age term $v\,t_{\text{age}}$ contributes `{python} SensorInformationAge.row_age_str` of blind displacement to the stopping distance derived in @eq-body-stopping-distance:
`{python} SensorInformationAge.d_stop_display_math`
This additional term raises the partial stopping distance from `{python} SensorInformationAge.total_before_str` to `{python} SensorInformationAge.total_after_str`. Although `{python} SensorInformationAge.remaining_str` remains within the nominal `{python} SensorInformationAge.d_clear_str` rack-end clearance, that remainder cannot be claimed as safety buffer: it must still absorb travel during planning admission $\Delta_{\text{da}}$, spatial tracking errors, and braking deceleration profiles. This analysis sizes the perception subsystem's contribution to the stopping budget and clarifies the empirical measurements required before an integrated motion claim can be certified.

| Stage              |                                       Increment |                                  Serial age after stage | What to verify                          |
|:-------------------|------------------------------------------------:|--------------------------------------------------------:|:----------------------------------------|
| Exposure midpoint  |  `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_exp_half_str` |  `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_exposure_str` | Exposure and row timestamp convention   |
| Rolling readout    |   `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_readout_str` |   `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_readout_str` | Selected row and overlap with streaming |
| Residual transport | `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_transport_str` | `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_transport_str` | Selected sensor mode and host receiver  |
| DMA and queue      |       `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_dma_str` |       `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_dma_str` | Arbitration and queue tail              |
| ISP                |       `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_isp_str` |       `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_isp_str` | Mode and competing jobs                 |
| Vision backbone    |  `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_backbone_str` |  `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_backbone_str` | Workload, clock, thermal state          |
| Dispatch           |       `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_ipc_str` |         **`{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str`** | Capture-to-dispatch age and queue tail  |

: **Serial information-age budget**: The navigation camera's stage increments, assumed nonoverlapping, sum to its observation age. A real pipeline can overlap readout, transfer, and processing, so capture-to-dispatch age requires an end-to-end measurement including queueing tails. Later consumers must add their elapsed post-dispatch interval. {#tbl-08-latency-budget tbl-colwidths="[24,18,20,38]"}

- [ ] **Pose propagation from capture time**: Can you explain how propagating the machine's pose forward from an observation's capture time places an old observation correctly in the current frame, and why that propagation cannot return the distance already traveled?

### Dating the machine's LiDAR {#sec-perception-lidar-age}

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-lidar-age
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LIDAR AGE AT THE RACK END: STREAMED SECTOR VS FULL SWEEP
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-perception-lidar-age and @tbl-08-lidar-age.
# │
# │ Goal:    Date the OS1-64's rack-end claim two ways and compare it with the
# │          navigation camera's dispatch age.
# │ Show:    the aisle ahead subtends 61.2 degrees, swept in 8.5 ms; age before
# │          processing 19.5 ms streamed vs 61.0 ms full sweep (with 10 ms data
# │          latency and a 1 ms PTP bound); 32.1 ms left for de-skew and
# │          occupancy extraction before the LiDAR claim is older than the
# │          camera's 51.6 ms.
# │ How:     RM.lidar.scan_rate; AISLE.aisle_width and AISLE.d_clear; Ouster OS1
# │          Rev7 datasheet data latency (< 10 ms) and PTP accuracy (< 1 ms)
# │          from the registry; AISLE.perception_age.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_length, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class LidarAge:
    """Age of the OS1-64's rack-end sector under two consumption policies."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_sweep = (1 / RM.lidar.scan_rate).to(millisecond)  # category: datasheet (20 Hz mode)
    aisle_width = AISLE.aisle_width  # category: illustrative
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    t_data = RM.lidar.nominal_latency.to(millisecond)  # category: datasheet (registry: OS1 Rev7 data latency upper bound)
    eps_ptp = RM.lidar.time_sync_accuracy.to(millisecond)  # category: datasheet (registry: OS1 Rev7 PTP accuracy upper bound)
    t_camera = AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond)  # category: derived
    v = RM.base.max_velocity.to(meter / second)  # category: illustrative (drive limit)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    half_width = (aisle_width / 2).to(meter)
    sector_deg = 2 * math.degrees(math.atan((half_width / d_clear).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude))
    t_sector = (t_sweep * sector_deg / 360.0).to(millisecond)
    age_stream = (t_sector + t_data + eps_ptp).to(millisecond)
    age_full = (t_sweep + t_data + eps_ptp).to(millisecond)
    dx_stream = (v * age_stream).to(ureg.millimeter)
    dx_full = (v * age_full).to(ureg.millimeter)
    slack_stream = (t_camera - age_stream).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(sector_deg - 61.2) < 0.05, f"Unexpected forward sector: {sector_deg}")
    check(abs(t_sector.magnitude - 8.5) < 0.05, f"Unexpected sector time: {t_sector}")
    check(abs(age_stream.magnitude - 19.5) < 0.05, f"Unexpected streamed age: {age_stream}")
    check(abs(age_full.magnitude - 61.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected full-sweep age: {age_full}")
    check(age_full > t_camera, "Prose says the full-sweep policy is older than the camera before processing")
    check(abs(slack_stream.magnitude - 32.1) < 0.05, f"Unexpected streamed slack: {slack_stream}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_sweep_str = fmt_latency(t_sweep, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    aisle_width_str = fmt_length(aisle_width.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    sector_deg_str = fmt(sector_deg, precision=1)
    t_sector_str = fmt_latency(t_sector, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_data_str = fmt_latency(t_data, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    eps_ptp_str = fmt_latency(eps_ptp, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    age_stream_str = fmt_latency(age_stream, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    age_full_str = fmt_latency(age_full, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    dx_stream_str = fmt_length(dx_stream, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    dx_full_str = fmt_length(dx_full, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    t_camera_str = fmt_latency(t_camera, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    slack_stream_str = fmt_latency(slack_stream, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

The safety verification path inspects range returns from the mobile base's Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR, whose timing structure differs fundamentally from that of the optical camera. A rolling-shutter camera exposes and reads out a discrete frame grid. In contrast, a spinning mechanical LiDAR continuously fires laser diodes and timestamps each azimuth column at the firing instant, disciplined by the IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (PTP). Because every point carries an individual capture epoch, the scan lacks a singular frame time. The age of the resulting rack-end spatial estimate is therefore governed by how long the software pipeline buffers returns before releasing the angular sector facing the hazard.

At the configured scan rate, one mechanical revolution requires `{python} LidarAge.t_sweep_str`. At a clear distance of `{python} LidarAge.d_clear_str`, the `{python} LidarAge.aisle_width_str` aisle subtends a forward azimuth sector of `{python} LidarAge.sector_deg_str`°, which the sensor sweeps in `{python} LidarAge.t_sector_str`. @Tbl-08-lidar-age compares two ingestion architectures for handling this point stream: streaming sector packets to consumers immediately upon arrival vs. buffering the entire sweep before dispatching a complete 360° point cloud.

| Stage                                    |              Stream the forward sector |              Wait for the full sweep | Source                             |
|:-----------------------------------------|---------------------------------------:|-------------------------------------:|:-----------------------------------|
| Acquisition of the oldest relevant point |       `{python} LidarAge.t_sector_str` |      `{python} LidarAge.t_sweep_str` | Scan rate and aisle geometry       |
| Sensor data latency, upper bound         |         `{python} LidarAge.t_data_str` |       `{python} LidarAge.t_data_str` | Datasheet                          |
| Clock-conversion bound (PTP)             |        `{python} LidarAge.eps_ptp_str` |      `{python} LidarAge.eps_ptp_str` | Datasheet; measure on the machine  |
| Upper age before processing              | **`{python} LidarAge.age_stream_str`** | **`{python} LidarAge.age_full_str`** | Computed                           |
| Travel at the drive limit                |      `{python} LidarAge.dx_stream_str` |      `{python} LidarAge.dx_full_str` | Computed                           |
| De-skew and occupancy extraction         |                   Needs measured value |                 Needs measured value | Host measurement under camera load |

: **LiDAR age at the rack end**: The OS1-64's upper age before host processing under two consumption policies, at the configured scan rate. Data latency and clock accuracy are the datasheet's upper bounds; processing time must be measured on the machine under the synchronized camera and inference load. {#tbl-08-lidar-age tbl-colwidths="[30,22,22,26]"}

Waiting for a full revolution renders the LiDAR observation `{python} LidarAge.age_full_str` old before host computation begins—already exceeding the camera's total dispatch age of `{python} LidarAge.t_camera_str`. In contrast, streaming the forward azimuth sector immediately leaves `{python} LidarAge.slack_stream_str` of timing headroom for motion de-skew and occupancy extraction before the LiDAR estimate lags behind the camera pipeline. The real-time latency budget dictates the architectural choice: the robot streams and processes sector packets incrementally, propagating individual point timestamps rather than a single aggregated sweep time. The stopping budget charges the camera's observation age because the motion planner anchors its trajectory proposal to the optical camera's frame epoch; the hardware safety monitor independently checks the LiDAR return age against a dedicated validity threshold once host processing latency is characterized. Note that neither ledger needs to calculate the internal latency of the certified optical safety scanner: its worst-case response time is a factory-certified parameter accounted for separately in the emergency stopping budget of @sec-enforcement-composite-budget. Per-column timestamps also enable continuous motion de-skew. Over a single LiDAR revolution at full speed, the mobile base translates `{python} LidarSweep.dx_sweep_str`; the state estimator eliminates this distortion by interpolating robot odometry at each return's precise firing timestamp (@sec-perception-transduction-calibration).

While the optical camera avoids rotational sweeping delays, its serial latency budget leaves zero slack for arbitrary queueing. In particular, collecting consecutive frames into multi-frame batches introduces substantial latency penalties before host memory contention is even considered.

### Temporal batching and feedback stability erosion

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-temporal-batching
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TEMPORAL BATCHING ON THE NAVIGATION CAMERA
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The temporal-batching paragraph of @sec-perception-photons-to-claims.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show what a four-frame batch collected across capture times adds
# │          to the navigation camera's observation age.
# │ Show:    16.7 ms frame period at 60 Hz; waits of 50.0, 33.3, and 16.7 ms;
# │          age 51.6 ms -> 101.6 ms, roughly double.
# │ How:     RM.nav_camera.frame_rate; AISLE.perception_age; the oldest of
# │          n frames waits (n - 1) frame periods.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class TemporalBatching:
    """Age added by batching successive navigation-camera frames."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    f_frame = RM.nav_camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond)  # category: derived
    n_batch = 4  # category: illustrative (batch size)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_period = (1 / f_frame).to(millisecond)
    wait_1 = ((n_batch - 1) * t_period).to(millisecond)
    wait_2 = ((n_batch - 2) * t_period).to(millisecond)
    wait_3 = ((n_batch - 3) * t_period).to(millisecond)
    t_age_batched = (t_age + wait_1).to(millisecond)
    ratio = (t_age_batched / t_age).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(f_frame.to(ureg.hertz).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected frame rate: {f_frame}")
    check(abs(wait_1.magnitude - 50.0) < 0.05, f"Unexpected oldest-frame wait: {wait_1}")
    check(abs(t_age_batched.magnitude - 101.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected batched age: {t_age_batched}")
    check(1.8 < ratio < 2.2, f"Prose says batching roughly doubles the age: {ratio}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    f_frame_str = fmt_frequency(f_frame, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    t_period_str = fmt_latency(t_period, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    wait_1_str = fmt_latency(wait_1, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    wait_2_str = fmt_latency(wait_2, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    wait_3_str = fmt_latency(wait_3, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_age_batched_str = fmt_latency(t_age_batched, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

Batching amortizes kernel launch overhead and maximizes systolic-array utilization on modern accelerators, but accumulating frames across successive capture times severely ages the earliest samples. At the navigation camera's `{python} TemporalBatching.f_frame_str` sampling rate ($T_{\text{sample}} \approx$ `{python} TemporalBatching.t_period_str`), forming a batch of four consecutive frames requires holding the first frame for `{python} TemporalBatching.wait_1_str`, the second for `{python} TemporalBatching.wait_2_str`, and the third for `{python} TemporalBatching.wait_3_str`, while only the fourth enters immediately. Appending this `{python} TemporalBatching.wait_1_str` queueing delay to the baseline `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.t_age_str` observation age roughly doubles total age to `{python} TemporalBatching.t_age_batched_str`. This staleness violates the local dispatch deadline established in @sec-perception-observation-contract, causing the perception record to fail its quality contract before candidate trajectory admission can even begin. When multi-camera systems synchronize exposure pulses in hardware, grouping frames from distinct sensors across spatial dimensions can improve throughput safely; however, temporal batching across successive timestamps directly erodes closed-loop timeliness.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-phase-margin-age
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PHASE MARGIN SPENT BY OBSERVATION AGE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The phase-margin paragraph of @sec-perception-photons-to-claims
# │          and its margin figure.
# │
# │ Goal:    Turn a nominal phase margin at crossover into the delay ceiling
# │          a pure age may spend, and show how much of it a 60 ms age uses.
# │ Show:    45 deg at 10 rad/s -> 78.5 ms ceiling; 60 ms uses 76.4 percent.
# │ How:     A pure delay tau removes phase omega_c * tau, so the ceiling is
# │          PM_nom / omega_c (@sec-appendix-control-zoh).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_percent, check

class PhaseMarginAge:
    """Delay ceiling set by a nominal phase margin at crossover."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    omega_c = 10.0  # category: illustrative (gain crossover, rad/s)
    pm_nom_deg = 45.0  # category: illustrative (nominal phase margin, degrees)
    t_used = 60.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (exposure, transport, and inference)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    pm_nom_rad = math.radians(pm_nom_deg)
    f_c = omega_c / (2 * math.pi)
    tau_max = (pm_nom_rad / omega_c * second).to(millisecond)
    frac_used = (t_used / tau_max).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(tau_max.magnitude - 78.54) < 0.01, f"Unexpected delay ceiling: {tau_max}")
    check(0.76 < frac_used < 0.77, f"Unexpected share of margin used: {frac_used}")
    check(t_used < tau_max, "The example age must sit below the ceiling")
    # margin_phase_margin_erosion_knee.svg fig-alt hand-types PM 45 degrees, 60 ms and 78.5 ms.
    check(pm_nom_deg == 45.0 and abs(t_used.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "Phase-margin margin labels drifted")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    omega_c_str = fmt(omega_c, precision=0)
    f_c_str = fmt(f_c, precision=1)
    pm_nom_deg_str = fmt(pm_nom_deg, precision=0)
    pm_nom_rad_str = fmt(pm_nom_rad, precision=3)
    tau_max_str = fmt_latency(tau_max, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_used_str = fmt_latency(t_used, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    frac_used_str = fmt(frac_used * 100, precision=1)
```

Beyond draining physical stopping distance, pipeline latency directly threatens closed-loop dynamic stability. Feedback control relies on negative feedback to damp tracking errors. If communication and inference delays postpone a control correction by half an oscillation period, the corrective effort arrives in phase with the motion it was designed to counteract. This phase inversion transforms stabilizing negative feedback into destabilizing positive feedback, causing the robot to weave across aisles, oscillate uncontrollably, or enter severe mechanical resonance.

In classical frequency-domain analysis, phase margin quantifies the maximum phase lag a stable feedback loop can absorb before becoming marginally stable. A pure delay $t_{\text{age}}$ introduces a frequency-dependent phase lag of $\theta(\omega) = \omega t_{\text{age}}$ radians without modifying system gain. A control loop with nominal phase margin $\text{PM}_{\text{nom}}$ evaluated at gain crossover frequency $\omega_c$[^fn-gain-crossover-margin] exhausts its stability reserve entirely when latency reaches $t_{\text{age}} \ge \text{PM}_{\text{nom}}/\omega_c$. Physical exposure, digital readout, bus transport, neural inference, and actuator communication all draw from this identical stability ceiling (@sec-appendix-control-zoh). For example, consider a visual-servoing tracking loop operating at crossover frequency $\omega_c =$ `{python} PhaseMarginAge.omega_c_str` rad/s (approximately `{python} PhaseMarginAge.f_c_str` Hz) with a nominal phase margin of $\text{PM}_{\text{nom}} =$ `{python} PhaseMarginAge.pm_nom_deg_str`$^\circ$ (`{python} PhaseMarginAge.pm_nom_rad_str` rad). Its maximum tolerable latency ceiling is $\tau_{\max} = \text{PM}_{\text{nom}}/\omega_c =$ `{python} PhaseMarginAge.tau_max_str`. If sensor exposure, transport, and neural inference consume `{python} PhaseMarginAge.t_used_str`, the perception pipeline consumes `{python} PhaseMarginAge.frac_used_str` percent of the loop's entire stability allowance before motor commands are even computed, leaving an underdamped system vulnerable to tracking oscillations.

[^fn-gain-crossover-margin]: **Gain Crossover**: Defined as the frequency where open-loop magnitude equals unity ($|L(j\omega_c)| = 1$), where phase margin measures clearance above $-180^\circ$ (@sec-nervous-time-constants-phase-lag). Because pure processing delay introduces a phase penalty of $\omega_c \tau$ radians without altering loop gain, crossover frequency remains constant while phase margin erodes linearly. The quotient $\text{PM}_{\text{nom}}/\omega_c$ therefore establishes a strict upper bound on allowable lumped pipeline latency. \index{Control!gain crossover}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_phase_margin_erosion_knee.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Line labeled PM 45 degrees falling linearly with age, with a dot marked 60 milliseconds, crossing a dashed zero line at a red dot marked 78.5 milliseconds; beyond it the line turns red in a light red region labeled chatter."}

*Delay spends phase margin linearly; at `{python} PhaseMarginAge.tau_max_str` none remains.*
:::

Both checks evaluate the same underlying physical delay: phase lag diminishes closed-loop dynamic stability, while physical displacement consumes forward clearance ($d_{\text{blind}} = v \cdot t_{\text{age}}$). Because these represent two distinct consequences of a single elapsed duration, engineers must evaluate each failure mode independently rather than double-counting the latency in the stopping budget. Rigorous capture timestamps, qualified reference frames, and explicit error bounds make these physical consequences observable throughout the software stack. Even when zero-copy DMA architectures eliminate intermediate buffer copies during host ingestion, memory controller arbitration and bus contention continue to introduce subtle waiting times.
## Ingestion Overhead and Memory Bus Contention {#sec-perception-cost-ingestion}

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-naive-ingestion-copies
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ NAIVE MULTI-CAMERA INGESTION COPY TRAFFIC
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The naive-baseline paragraph of @sec-perception-cost-ingestion.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size the copy traffic when four 1080p60 RGB streams are copied
# │          three times on their way to the accelerator.
# │ Show:    4 x 1920 x 1080 x 3 B x 60 Hz = 1.5 GB/s per copy; 4.5 GB/s total.
# │ How:     rate = cameras x pixels x bytes/pixel x frame rate x copies.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_frequency, check

class NaiveIngestionCopies:
    """Copy traffic of a naive user-space multi-camera ingestion path."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    n_cam = 4  # category: illustrative (camera count)
    px = 1920 * 1080  # category: definitional (1080p frame)
    bytes_px = 3  # category: illustrative (24-bit RGB after conversion)
    f_cam = 60.0 * ureg.hertz  # category: illustrative (frame rate)
    n_copies = 3  # category: illustrative (driver ring, user space, device memory)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    per_copy = (n_cam * px * bytes_px * ureg.byte * f_cam).to(ureg.gigabyte / second)
    total = (per_copy * n_copies).to(ureg.gigabyte / second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(per_copy.magnitude - 1.493) < 0.01, f"Unexpected per-copy rate: {per_copy}")
    check(total > 4.0 * ureg.gigabyte / second, f"Unexpected total copy rate: {total}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    f_cam_str = fmt_frequency(f_cam, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    per_copy_str = fmt_bandwidth(per_copy, unit=ureg.gigabyte / second, precision=1)
    total_str = fmt_bandwidth(total, unit=ureg.gigabyte / second, precision=1)
```

A common architectural pitfall in early physical AI prototypes is connecting multiple high-resolution cameras through standard USB or Ethernet ports and ingesting frames using naive user-space libraries, such as OpenCV's `VideoCapture` or default ROS image transport nodes. In this unoptimized baseline, every incoming frame is copied from kernel USB request blocks into a driver ring buffer, copied a second time into user-space process memory, and copied a third time across the PCIe bus into GPU memory. For four 1080p cameras streaming 24-bit color at `{python} NaiveIngestionCopies.f_cam_str`, each copy stage moves `{python} NaiveIngestionCopies.per_copy_str`, meaning the pipeline churns through about `{python} NaiveIngestionCopies.total_str` of continuous memory copies. This overhead generates substantial memory traffic and CPU copying work, though the exact utilization depends on host core capabilities, memory architecture, and pixel format. That data rate alone does not establish CPU saturation or accelerator starvation, but it wastes memory bus bandwidth and cache capacity that concurrent real-time inference urgently requires.

Real-time physical systems avoid this collapse by treating pixel ingestion as a zero-copy DMA\index{Memory!DMA} hardware pipeline. Raw pixel streams arriving over dedicated camera buses bypass CPU copying entirely, writing frames directly into shared physical DRAM before any software thread touches the data.
