Against glass walls or metal structures, multi-bounce reflections cause emitted pulses to travel indirect paths back to the receiver, generating phantom point clusters that appear meters behind physical walls or deep beneath the concrete floor.

Millimeter-wave radar provides complementary all-weather capability that overcomes many optical failure modes. Operating at $76\text{ to }81\text{ GHz}$, frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar uses a carrier wavelength of $\lambda \approx 3.9\text{ mm}$—roughly 4,000 times larger than near-infrared laser pulses and several orders of magnitude larger than fog droplets ($1\text{ to }10\,\mu\text{m}$). Scattering by such small airborne particles falls squarely within the Rayleigh scattering regime, where the particle scattering cross-section $\sigma_s$ scales inversely with the fourth power of wavelength:
$$\sigma_s \propto \frac{d_{\text{droplet}}^6}{\lambda^4}$$
Although this extreme wavelength dependence shields radar from the severe attenuation and backscatter that paralyze optical sensors in fog and dust, radar is not immune to environmental interference. Ground reflections produce multipath ghost detections, standing water films on the radome attenuate radio-frequency signals, and low spatial resolution complicates boundary discrimination. A multimodal perception suite must therefore explicitly qualify radar coverage boundaries when primary optical streams degrade.

### Out-of-distribution inputs at the sensor boundary

Even when a sensor is calibrated, unoccluded, and operating without transport faults, its observations can fall outside the operational distribution on which downstream models were qualified. Uncertainty in these observations stems from two distinct sources. **Aleatoric uncertainty**\index{Uncertainty!aleatoric} represents the irreducible physical noise of the transduction process itself—such as photon shot noise, thermal amplifier noise, or aerosol backscatter. The measurement's covariance model must quantify this uncertainty. In contrast, **epistemic uncertainty**\index{Uncertainty!epistemic} stems from the model's lack of knowledge about scenarios omitted from its training distribution, such as an overturned forklift, an unfamiliar emergency strobe pattern, or a dense chemical vapor plume. Upgrading sensor fidelity cannot eliminate epistemic uncertainty. The theoretical limits of normalized softmax scores and methods for calibrated uncertainty estimation are analyzed in @sec-brain-softmax-illusion, while the conversion of calibrated prediction sets into action refusals is treated in @eq-intent-conformal-set. Perception carries a specific, narrower engineering responsibility: it must determine at the ingestion boundary whether an incoming observation falls outside the validated input support, and log that assessment directly in the observation record.

Input-support monitors evaluate incoming sensor frames—or early feature embeddings from the neural backbone—against the support of the qualification dataset. Common implementations include computing a free-energy score over unnormalized logits [@liu2020energy], measuring the Mahalanobis distance to class-conditional feature centroids [@lee2018simple], or tracking the reconstruction error of an autoencoder trained strictly on nominal operational data. Each method requires an empirical acceptance threshold calibrated against expected anomalies. However, an in-bounds score guarantees only that an input resembles the training distribution, not that the network's semantic inference is physically accurate. These checks instantiate the input-support monitor formalized in @sec-evaluation-limits.

When an input-support monitor detects an anomaly, the perception pipeline sets the `BIT_OOD_DETECTED` flag in the observation record's health bitmask. The safety permission path monitors this bitmask to disallow high-speed motions, expand conservative clearance buffers, or trigger a deterministic supervisory fallback. In multimodal systems, this bitmask orchestrates cross-modal arbitration: if an optical camera raises `BIT_OPTICAL_SATURATED` or `BIT_OOD_DETECTED` while an FMCW radar reports coherent Doppler returns, the fusion pipeline demotes optical tokens and relies primarily on radar range estimates, provided the radar modality is independently validated to enforce spatial clearance under those operating conditions.

::: {#ws-perception-tesla-williston-omission .callout-war-story title="Silent perception omission (2016)"}
**Context**: A 2015 Tesla Model S\index{Incidents!Williston accident} traveling at about $74\text{ mph}$ with Traffic-Aware Cruise Control and Autosteer active struck a refrigerated semitrailer turning left across its path near Williston, Florida [@ntsb2017tesla].

**Mechanism**: The crossing-path collision lay outside the front-to-rear crash modes for which the 2015 warning and automatic braking systems were designed. NHTSA reported that automatic braking required agreement between camera and radar; unusual vehicle shapes could impede camera classification ([NHTSA ODI PE16-007](https://static.nhtsa.gov/odi/inv/2016/INCLA-PE16007-7876.PDF)).

**Impact**: The NTSB found no recorded indication that forward collision warning or automatic emergency braking detected an object, and no pre-impact braking occurred. The vehicle passed beneath the turning semitrailer, shearing off the car's roof; the paired investigation photographs in @fig-08-real-ntsb-williston-crash document this physical outcome, highlighting collision scrape damage along the right underside of the trailer alongside the roofless passenger cabin.

**Response**: The NTSB examined operational design domain limits and driver engagement as well as the collision-avoidance systems.

**Systems lesson**: An absent detection is not evidence that a crossing path is clear. A permission design must account for detection coverage and unsupported scenarios; a health flag cannot certify that every relevant object was perceived.
:::

::: {#fig-08-real-ntsb-williston-crash fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Williston collision damage**: This NTSB presentation slide shows damage on the right side of the semitrailer and the roofless Tesla after the 2016 crash. The crossing-path geometry and absence of pre-impact braking come from the [NTSB accident report](https://www.ntsb.gov/investigations/AccidentReports/Reports/HAR1702.pdf), not from the photographs alone. (Source: NTSB board-meeting presentation for report HAR-17/02; photographs courtesy of Florida Highway Patrol)." fig-alt="NTSB slide with two photographs: left, a refrigerated semitrailer with damage low on its right side; right, a heavily damaged roofless Tesla. Yellow ovals mark damage areas. The photos do not show the vehicles' motion or collision angle."}
![](images/png/fig08_real_ntsb_williston_crash.png){width="90%"}
:::

Ultimately, an observation record can expose only the physical, temporal, and distributional faults that the ingestion layer is designed to measure. Detectable interface errors, transport jitter, and out-of-distribution feature shifts are readily encoded into explicit health bitmasks. Yet silent semantic omissions—such as the missed detection at Williston—inevitably evade single-sensor health checks. Preventing catastrophic failures requires an architectural safety design: incorporating independent physical sensing modalities, enforcing conservative spatial permission envelopes, and never mistaking the absence of an error flag for confirmation of physical safety.
## The Observation Contract {#sec-perception-observation-contract}

A downstream tracker, policy backbone, or permission path cannot reconstruct exposure timing, mounting calibration, or byte integrity from a raw tensor alone. The perception subsystem therefore wraps each sensory output in an **observation contract**\index{Observation contract!definition}\index{Perception!observation contract}, the sixth record in the book's fifteen-record chain. In closed-loop physical systems, an observation is unusable without an explicit capture epoch, an identified clock domain, a bounded conversion to the permission path's clock, and an extrinsic calibration operating within its qualified validity envelope. A safe consumer must reject any incoming record lacking these guarantees before inspecting a single payload byte. The system's shared clock domain and $\mathcal{H}_1$ age budget originate in the nervous-system handoff record of @sec-nervous-handoffs-matrix; perception, in turn, provides the capture-side timestamps and uncertainty bounds that downstream consumers need to verify compliance.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-handoff-sensor-age
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SENSOR-SIDE AGE AGAINST THE H_1 HANDOFF ALLOTMENT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The handoff paragraph of @sec-perception-observation-contract.
# │
# │ Goal:    Reconcile the handoff matrix's sensor-age allotment (one frame
# │          period) with this chapter's exposure-midpoint-plus-readout age.
# │ Show:    16.7 ms frame period; 24.6 ms from the top row's exposure midpoint
# │          to the end of readout; 16.3 ms from the middle row's; the top-row
# │          convention exceeds the allotment by 7.9 ms.
# │ How:     RM.nav_camera frame rate, exposure, and readout. The allotment is
# │          taken as one frame period, matching the handoff matrix value.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class HandoffSensorAge:
    """Sensor-side age of the navigation camera under two row conventions."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    camera = RM.nav_camera  # category: datasheet (registry: navigation camera)
    t_exp = camera.exposure_time.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen (configured exposure)
    t_readout = camera.readout_time.to(millisecond)  # category: datasheet
    f_frame = camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_frame = (1 / f_frame).to(millisecond)
    age_top = (t_exp / 2 + t_readout).to(millisecond)
    age_mid = (t_exp / 2 + t_readout / 2).to(millisecond)
    excess_top = (age_top - t_frame).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_frame.magnitude - 16.7) < 0.05, f"Unexpected frame period: {t_frame}")
    check(abs(age_top.magnitude - 24.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected top-row sensor age: {age_top}")
    check(abs(age_mid.magnitude - 16.3) < 0.05, f"Unexpected middle-row sensor age: {age_mid}")
    check(age_mid < t_frame < age_top, "Prose says only the middle-row convention fits the allotment")
    check(abs(excess_top.magnitude - 7.9) < 0.05, f"Unexpected excess: {excess_top}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_frame_str = fmt_latency(t_frame, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    f_frame_str = fmt_frequency(f_frame, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    age_top_str = fmt_latency(age_top, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    age_mid_str = fmt_latency(age_mid, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    excess_top_str = fmt_latency(excess_top, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

Formally, the contract couples either a raw observation tensor or an extracted geometric bounding envelope with the validation metadata that downstream consumers require (@eq-percep-observation-contract-tuple):
$$\mathcal{O} = \langle t_{\text{capture}}, \text{clock\_id}, \epsilon_{\text{sync}}, \text{frame\_id}, \mathbf{T}_{\text{payload}}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, C_{\text{inset}}, \text{mask}_{\text{health}}, \text{crc32} \rangle$$ {#eq-percep-observation-contract-tuple}
In this tuple, $t_{\text{capture}}$ records the exposure-midpoint timestamp registered on monotonic clock $\text{clock\_id}$, $\epsilon_{\text{sync}}$ bounds the maximum synchronization error when converting to the safety controller's clock, and $\text{frame\_id}$ identifies the calibrated sensor transform. The payload $\mathbf{T}_{\text{payload}}$ contains the raw sensor array or derived geometric bounding envelope, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ characterizes its spatial covariance, $C_{\text{inset}}$ provides the qualified clearance inset, $\text{mask}_{\text{health}}$ conveys hardware and perceptual health status bits, and $\text{crc32}$ seals both header and payload against transport corruption. Spatial memory (@sec-memory) consumes this record to update its world model, while trajectory planning (@sec-planning) uses $C_{\text{inset}}$ to inflate collision boundaries; both modules evaluate evidence age, verify kinematic coordinate frames, and bound spatial uncertainty before allowing an observation to influence a control decision.

This contract does not replace binary serialization formats such as Protocol Buffers, FlatBuffers, or ROS 2 IDL. In fact, any of these serialization systems can transmit the underlying struct over shared memory or bus fabrics. While transport schemas standardize memory layout and data types, the observation contract establishes verifiable physical invariants: monotonic temporal progression, bounded clock skew, active calibration validity windows, and rigorous spatial uncertainty limits. @Tbl-08-observation-record-schema details each field alongside its validation rule and populates the schema for the mobile manipulator's navigation camera.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-nav-observation-record
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ NAVIGATION-CAMERA OBSERVATION RECORD, FILLED
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The filled column of @tbl-08-observation-record-schema and the
# │          clock-conversion paragraph that follows it.
# │
# │ Goal:    Fill the observation record for the mobile manipulator's
# │          navigation camera and size the consumer's upper age at dispatch.
# │ Show:    age at dispatch 51.6 ms; clock-conversion bound 0.2 ms; upper
# │          age 51.8 ms, equal to the refusal threshold (budgeted age plus
# │          bound); frame counter at 60 Hz; the bound's 0.3 mm of travel at
# │          the 1.5 m/s drive limit, carried inside delta_loc rather than
# │          charged as a budget row.
# │ How:     AISLE.perception_age (the latency waterfall above); eps_sync is a
# │          chapter LOAD value that the spatial-belief record of @sec-memory
# │          reuses; RM.nav_camera frame rate; displacement via
# │          calc_spatial_information_age_displacement.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, fmt_length, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class NavObservationRecord:
    """Filled observation record for the running machine's navigation camera."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    camera = RM.nav_camera  # category: datasheet (registry: Sony IMX477 navigation camera)
    f_frame = camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond)  # category: derived
    eps_sync = 0.2 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (capture-to-MCU clock-conversion bound; reused by @sec-memory)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity.to(meter / second)  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    upper_age = (t_age + eps_sync).to(millisecond)
    refuse_threshold = (AISLE.perception_age + eps_sync).to(millisecond)  # refusal threshold: budgeted age plus the conversion bound
    dx_sync = calc_spatial_information_age_displacement(v, eps_sync).to(ureg.millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_age.magnitude - 51.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected age at dispatch: {t_age}")
    check(abs(eps_sync.to(millisecond).magnitude - 0.2) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected clock-conversion bound: {eps_sync}")
    check(abs(upper_age.magnitude - 51.8) < 0.05, f"Unexpected upper age at dispatch: {upper_age}")
    check(abs(refuse_threshold.magnitude - 51.8) < 0.05, f"Unexpected refusal threshold: {refuse_threshold}")
    check(abs((refuse_threshold - upper_age).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Prose says the dispatched upper age meets the refusal threshold exactly")
    check(abs(f_frame.to(ureg.hertz).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected navigation-camera frame rate: {f_frame}")
    check(abs(dx_sync.magnitude - 0.3) < 0.005, f"Unexpected travel during the clock-conversion bound: {dx_sync}")
    check(dx_sync < delta_loc, "Prose says the clock-conversion travel fits inside delta_loc")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    eps_sync_str = fmt_latency(eps_sync.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    upper_age_str = fmt_latency(upper_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    refuse_threshold_str = fmt_latency(refuse_threshold, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    f_frame_str = fmt_frequency(f_frame, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    dx_sync_str = fmt_length(dx_sync, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
```

| Record field                               | Meaning                                                           | Consumer check                                                                                     | Navigation camera                                                                                                                                                        |
|:-------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `capture_timestamp_ns`, `capture_clock_id` | Exposure midpoint in one shared, monotonic capture clock          | Convert to safety microcontroller (MCU) time with a valid bounded-skew mapping before checking age | Trigger edge plus $t_{\text{exp}}/2$ (top-row exposure midpoint) on clock `cam_nav`; dispatched `{python} NavObservationRecord.t_age_str` later (@tbl-08-latency-budget) |
| `sync_error_ns`                            | Bound on capture-to-MCU clock conversion error                    | Add to worst-case age; refuse if missing or expired                                                | `{python} NavObservationRecord.eps_sync_str`, so the upper age at dispatch is `{python} NavObservationRecord.upper_age_str`                                              |
| `sequence_index`                           | Monotonic camera frame counter                                    | Detect gaps and reordering                                                                         | One count per frame at `{python} NavObservationRecord.f_frame_str`                                                                                                       |
| `sensor_frame_id`                          | Transform-tree key and calibration revision                       | Select the valid extrinsic transform                                                               | `nav_cam` with its calibration revision                                                                                                                                  |
| `tensor_payload`                           | Format, dimensions, length, and buffer                            | Validate bounds and record checksum before reading                                                 | Raw/debayered image tensor or point-cloud buffer                                                                                                                         |
| `bounding_envelope`                        | Bounding volume $[dx, dy, dz]$ or qualified clearance inset       | Bound occupied volume and inflate safety sets ($C_{\text{inset}}$)                                 | Metric corridor bounds inflated by validated quantile                                                                                                                    |
| `spatial_covariance`                       | Positive-semidefinite spatial error scale                         | Use with separately calibrated bias and tail bounds                                                | Point-wise or object-centric covariance matrix $\mathbf{\Sigma}_z$                                                                                                       |
| `calibration_metadata`                     | Intrinsics, extrinsics, coefficients, temperature, validity range | Reject calibration outside its validated region                                                    | Factory pinhole $\mathbf{K}$ and chassis extrinsic transform $\mathbf{T}_{bc}$                                                                                           |
| `provenance_digest`                        | SHA-256 of firmware and model revisions                           | Match the approved build; this is not payload integrity                                            | Signed hash of vision backbone weights and firmware                                                                                                                      |
| `payload_crc32`                            | CRC over serialized header (excluding this field) and payload     | Detect accidental record corruption; not authentication                                            | 32-bit cyclical redundancy check                                                                                                                                         |
| `health_bitmask`                           | Hardware, degradation, and perception validity flags              | Refuse claims with safety-critical faults or OOD flags                                             | Sync-loss, link, saturation, rain/fog clutter, and OOD bits; input-support bits from @sec-evaluation-limits                                                              |

: **Observation contract schema**: Compact fields needed to date and frame a claim, evaluate its uncertainty, bounding envelope, and health flags, and check the bytes and generating revision. The last column fills the fields this chapter computes for the mobile manipulator's navigation camera; its dispatch age and clock-conversion bound are illustrative. A keyed authenticator is a separate requirement if the threat model includes malicious modification. {#tbl-08-observation-record-schema tbl-colwidths="[23,23,26,28]"}

The fields detailed in @tbl-08-observation-record-schema anchor each observation in physical time, geometric space, and software revision history. The capture timestamp $t_{\text{capture}}$ must refer to a strictly monotonic hardware timer rather than wall-clock time (such as nanoseconds since the UNIX epoch), which remains vulnerable to stepping backward during network time adjustments. Because rolling-shutter sensors read out scan lines sequentially, any spatial claim derived from a rolling-shutter imager must explicitly identify the image row or region corresponding to that capture instant. The transport-level `sequence_index` counter detects frame drops and out-of-order deliveries directly on the bus, independently of clock readings. When the safety microcontroller (MCU) operates in a separate clock domain from the camera host, an active synchronization daemon provides a versioned affine mapping $t_{\text{MCU}} = a t_{\text{capture}} + b$, an expiration window, and an empirical sync-error bound $\epsilon_{\text{sync}}$, characterized as described in @sec-perception-qualifying-error.

Systems engineering demands precise conventions when accounting for sensor latency. The handoff matrix and the perception pipeline ledger evaluate the sensor's latency contribution under different row conventions, and the observation contract must explicitly state which convention governs the record. The handoff matrix allots $\mathcal{H}_1$ an allowance of one frame period—`{python} HandoffSensorAge.t_frame_str` at `{python} HandoffSensorAge.f_frame_str`—and references the entire frame by its middle row. Measuring from that middle row's exposure midpoint to the completion of sensor readout yields a sensor-side latency of $t_{\text{exp}}/2 + t_{\text{readout}}/2 =$ `{python} HandoffSensorAge.age_mid_str`, which falls well within the handoff allotment. Conversely, the perception latency waterfall charges for the top row: $t_{\text{exp}}/2 + t_{\text{readout}} =$ `{python} HandoffSensorAge.age_top_str`. Because a physical hazard such as a warehouse rack upright can appear in the very first scan lines, a safety-certified stopping budget must charge for the oldest sensory evidence underpinning the spatial claim. Under this oldest-row convention, the navigation camera exceeds the handoff allotment by `{python} HandoffSensorAge.excess_top_str`. Both figures are mathematically valid within their respective contexts: the middle-row convention models typical tracking latency, while the oldest-row convention guarantees safety for worst-case stopping distances. Stamping the reference row index directly into the capture metadata allows downstream consumers to translate between these conventions without ambiguity.

Upon dispatching an observation, the producer records an upper bound on evidence age as $t_{\text{MCU,dispatch}} - t_{\text{MCU,capture}} + \epsilon_{\text{sync}}$. That metric reflects only the latency accumulated up to the producer's egress boundary. By the time the safety checker or trajectory validator admits the record, the evidence has aged further by the dispatch-to-admission transit delay $\Delta_{\text{da}}$, and it ages further still before actuators execute a command. The permission path must evaluate freshness using its local monotonic clock against the original capture epoch; treating a static dispatch timestamp as if time had frozen violates basic physical causality. Submitting a new trajectory proposal derived from a previously buffered observation does not refresh the underlying sensory evidence.

For the navigation camera, the **dispatch-local** threshold equals the nominal perception pipeline latency `{python} NavObservationRecord.t_age_str` plus the `{python} NavObservationRecord.eps_sync_str` clock-conversion bound, yielding `{python} NavObservationRecord.refuse_threshold_str`. The nominal frame hits this threshold precisely at dispatch, leaving zero spare margin for host contention, pipeline queuing, or batching delays. In the vehicle's dynamic stopping ledger, the `{python} NavObservationRecord.t_age_str` perception delay maps directly to physical travel distance at cruising velocity, while the `{python} NavObservationRecord.dx_sync_str` displacement associated with the clock-conversion uncertainty bound is absorbed into the localization uncertainty parameter $\delta_{\text{loc}}$. Neither accounting choice eliminates the ongoing physical aging that occurs after dispatch.

Admitting an observation into the motion-planning safety pipeline requires an empirically qualified current-age limit that accounts for the dispatch-to-admission bound $\Delta_{\text{da}}$ while reserving sufficient execution time for the active motion lease and physical braking response. Because this partial systems ledger has not yet bounded $\Delta_{\text{da}}$, the populated record in @tbl-08-observation-record-schema illustrates correct structural field construction rather than an admitted full-speed trajectory. Once engineers measure and bound $\Delta_{\text{da}}$ across all inter-process channels, they can either close the formal stopping distance ledger or reduce maximum vehicle velocity to restore safety margins. Systems latency accounting requires strict conservation of time: whether an engineer anchors the timeline at physical capture or measures from the admission gate by summing prior evidence age with the active lease, each elapsed interval appears exactly once in the safety ledger.

The transform identifier `sensor_frame_id` and its calibration revision key the observation into the robot's kinematic transform tree.[^fn-stereo-baseline-thermal] The provenance digest records the exact SHA-256 hash of the vision model weights and camera firmware, providing an auditable record of software configuration. Concurrently, `payload_crc32` guards against transmission glitches across shared-memory rings or serial buses. Systems designers must distinguish data integrity from semantic truth: checksums and build digests detect accidental bit flips and firmware mismatches, but they cannot verify whether an image is optically uncorrupted, nor do they prevent adversarial tampering without a keyed cryptographic signature.

[^fn-stereo-baseline-thermal]: **Stereo Baseline Thermal Drift**\index{Hardware!thermal expansion}: For a stereo baseline $b =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.b_str` and an unmodeled change $|\delta b| =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.db_str`, first-order geometry gives $|\delta z|/z\approx|\delta b|/b$. At $z =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.z_thermal_str`, the corresponding depth bias is about `{python} StereoDepthError.dz_thermal_str`, assuming focal length and disparity are otherwise unchanged. Temperature compensation must be checked against the actual mount and calibration.

The `health_bitmask` structures failure reporting across three architectural layers. The lowest bits report hardware-level faults, such as clock synchronization loss, DMA ring buffer overruns, or physical link dropouts. The intermediate bits signal environmental degradation, including sensor saturation from direct sunlight, optical blooming, and aerosol backscatter from dust or fog. The upper bits represent perceptual validity concerns, such as severe field-of-view occlusion or out-of-distribution (OOD) sensory inputs that fall outside the training support tested during system evaluation. These input-support bits directly instantiate the runtime monitoring mechanisms formalized in @sec-evaluation-limits. When any safety-critical bit is set, downstream motion planners and trackers must immediately reject spatial claims derived from that frame.

An explicit observation schema also creates a systematic interface for automated fault injection. Verification harnesses can deterministically alter capture timestamps, drop sequence numbers, artificially inflate covariance diagonals, or assert occlusion bits, confirming that downstream consumers reject or gracefully degrade unviable observations within their budgeted time limits. These software mutations prove that consumer software responds properly to corrupted contracts; evaluating resilience against real-world physical phenomena—such as optical flare, mounting deflection, and actuator dynamics—requires the hardware-in-the-loop testing regimes described in @sec-verification.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Observation contract mutations feed the hardware-in-the-loop verification harness in @sec-verification-hardware-fault-injection.
:::

Learned policies require explicit contract metadata just as much as classical state estimators do. An end-to-end policy $\mathbf{a}_t = \pi(\mathbf{z}_{t_0})$ that receives only sensory pixels or point clouds cannot distinguish two identical images consumed under radically different pipeline latencies. Widely used vision-language-action (VLA) models ignore this physical reality: architectures such as RT-2 and OpenVLA condition purely on visual tokens and natural language prompts [@brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla], while models like $\pi_0$ introduce proprioceptive joint telemetry [@black2024pi0] but still omit capture age, extrinsic transforms, and spatial measurement covariance. To integrate learned models safely into real-time control loops, this book presents an **observation tokenizer** that projects the full observation contract into the token space of a VLA policy or neural estimator. The sensory modality dictates the raw payload encoding—whether patch tokens from vision transformers, range tokens from lidar arrays, temporal spike tokens from event cameras, or stress fields from tactile arrays—while the unified tokenizer interface preserves the capture epoch, geometric frame, and measurement uncertainty associated with that payload.

Under this architecture, the observation tokenizer pairs the sensory feature tokens $\mathbf{z}_{\text{sensor}}$ with continuous Fourier temporal embeddings ($\mathbf{e}_{\Delta t} = \text{Fourier}(t_{\text{current}} - t_0)$), coordinate frame prefix embeddings ($\mathbf{e}_{\text{frame}} = \text{MLP}(\mathbf{T}_{bc})$), and spatial covariance embeddings ($\mathbf{e}_{\Sigma} = \text{MLP}(\text{vec}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_z))$) (@eq-percep-vla-obs-tokenizer):
$$\mathbf{z}_{\text{token}} = [\mathbf{z}_{\text{sensor}}, \mathbf{e}_{\Delta t}, \mathbf{e}_{\text{frame}}, \mathbf{e}_{\Sigma}]$$ {#eq-percep-vla-obs-tokenizer}
A forward-propagated state token $\mathbf{e}_{\text{state}} = \text{MLP}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{\text{current}}})$, generated by the state estimator in @sec-perception-state-estimation, can accompany these tokens so the policy conditions on the robot's predicted state at the instant of actuation rather than its historical configuration at sensor exposure. While this embedding scheme exposes physical time, frame geometry, and uncertainty directly to transformer attention layers, engineers must verify that the model actually attends to these tokens in closed-loop operation. Demonstrating that a policy leverages temporal embeddings requires rigorous ablation experiments that inject artificial latency into held-out evaluation trials and measure resulting closed-loop tracking error. Furthermore, embedding metadata as neural tokens does not substitute for deterministic safety gating: the permission path must continue to verify clock bounds, extrinsic calibration envelopes, innovation residuals, and health status bits before any network output is permitted to drive the physical actuators.

::: {#chk-percep-observation-contract-triage .callout-checkpoint title="Observation record checks"}

A consumer can refuse only what the record lets it check, and it must check before it reads the payload.

- [ ] **Record triage**: Can you explain why a health bit, checksum, valid clock conversion, and freshness check must precede consumption of a spatial claim?
- [ ] **Timestamp corruption vs. dropped packets**: Can you describe why receiving a sensory frame with a desynchronized timestamp degrades spatial state estimation and policy grounding far more severely than dropping the packet entirely?
- [ ] **Deterministic fault injection**: Can you distinguish between physically perturbing optical sensors vs. deterministically mutating fields in the shared-memory observation record during automated hardware-in-the-loop verification?
- [ ] **Batch-age estimate**: If the navigation camera's frames were batched in pairs at its `{python} TemporalBatching.f_frame_str` cadence, what would the older frame's dispatch age be, and would it meet the `{python} NavObservationRecord.refuse_threshold_str` dispatch-local threshold?

:::

Because the observation contract preserves the exact capture epoch, delayed frames do not become worthless garbage. When network congestion or compute preemption delays delivery, a state estimator can ingest an out-of-order observation at the precise historical instant it captured and propagate corrections forward to the current state, a technique explored in @sec-perception-discrete-state-estimation. Nevertheless, successfully passing contract triage and computing state updates does not make an observation semantically true in the physical world. The following common pitfalls illustrate how systems engineers confuse syntactically validated records with genuine physical reality.
## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-perception-fallacies-pitfalls}

Perception\index{Perception} must describe the physical world within the strict temporal deadlines demanded by closed-loop control. In embodied systems, high semantic confidence and fine spatial resolution cannot compensate for pipelines that deliver stale observations, fuse asynchronous exposures, or treat average I/O bandwidth as a bound on single-frame latency.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Accepting an observation because its semantic classification confidence is high, regardless of its age.*

Consider a mobile manipulator that receives an observation indicating with high semantic confidence that the rack end ahead is clear. If a scheduling stall in the vision pipeline\index{Perception!pipeline latency} delivers that observation several frames late, a warehouse worker who stepped into the aisle after the camera exposure will not appear in the image. The confidence score\index{Confidence score} describes only the classifier's assessment of past sensory input, not current physical clearance. Treating an overdue packet as present state risks commanding actuators directly into occupied space. The perception interface must verify measurement age against its freshness limit (@sec-perception-observation-contract)\index{Observation!freshness limit} and reject observations that exceed the threshold. Furthermore, any state propagation\index{State estimation!propagation} that continues without fresh data must inflate kinematic uncertainty covariances\index{Kinematics!uncertainty}, incorporating heavy-tailed residuals or reachability bounds on dynamic obstacles. This growth forces downstream controllers to contract their safety envelopes\index{Safety!envelope} and slow the robot as sensory evidence ages. High softmax confidence reflects internal model certainty on an acquired image, but it guarantees neither temporal freshness nor true physical clearance.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Fusing multi-sensor observations without a clock bound derived from the tolerated spatial error.*

Suppose two cameras on the mobile manipulator observe the same rack upright while the mobile base travels at its `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.v_str` velocity limit, but their internal clocks differ by an uncorrected skew $\Delta t_{\text{skew}}$. If downstream fusion treats the two exposure times\index{Exposure time} as simultaneous, the physical upright appears displaced by $v\,\Delta t_{\text{skew}}$ between the two sensor frames. Downstream track association\index{Track association} can split this single physical obstacle into two conflicting tracks ("ghosting"), corrupting the world model. Spatial calibration\index{Calibration!spatial} cannot correct an uncharacterized temporal offset. Instead, the allowable clock synchronization error must follow directly from the tolerated spatial position error $\epsilon_{\text{pos}}$ and the maximum operational velocity $v_{\text{max}}$, yielding the relation $\Delta t_{\text{skew}} \le \epsilon_{\text{pos}} / v_{\text{max}}$. Hardware synchronization\index{Hardware!clock synchronization} at exposure time makes that bound enforceable. Selecting a network timing technology—such as IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (PTP)\index{IEEE 1588 PTP}—without first deriving this spatial error budget leaves the sensor fusion pipeline ungrounded.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Inferring a critical read's deadline from average camera bandwidth.*

A comfortable average utilization figure says nothing about how long a critical read stalls behind synchronized sensor capture and inference bursts. On the mobile manipulator, safety permission checks execute on a dedicated real-time microcontroller reading from local memory, shielding the immediate control path from host bus contention. The danger instead appears on the application processor: concurrent DMA transfers, memory bus saturation, and inference bursts delay the sensor ingestion pipeline (@sec-perception-cost-ingestion). This contention inflates the capture-to-dispatch latency of the perceptual state estimate and stretches the renewal interval between successive updates. System architects must verify worst-case capture-to-dispatch age and end-to-end renewal intervals under peak burst conditions rather than relying on average throughput metrics.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Assuming an end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy implicitly learns to compensate for rolling shutter and sensor latency without explicit temporal tokenization.*

Deep imitation learning often assumes that large Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies trained on extensive robot teleoperation datasets will automatically learn action corrections that compensate for sensor distortion and communication latency. In practice, demonstration datasets aggregate trajectories collected across fluctuating chassis velocities, camera frame rates, and host bus loads. If the model receives only raw pixel arrays without capture timestamps or row readout schedules, it cannot distinguish true physical obstacle geometry from rolling-shutter scanline shear or motion lag. Unresolved temporal ambiguity degrades closed-loop trajectory tracking and induces control oscillations. The classic behavior-cloning bound of $O(T^2 \epsilon)$ characterizes compounding trajectory divergence across time horizon $T$ given per-step imitation error $\epsilon$, but it assumes a stationary Markovian process rather than unmodeled phase lags and sensor dynamics. Providing explicit timing metadata—such as capture time deltas ($\Delta t = t_{\text{current}} - t_0$), readout offsets, and forward-propagated kinematic states—gives the network the causal context required to resolve these distortions. Even with temporal tokenization, empirical evaluation must verify closed-loop stability, and independent out-of-band safety permission checks remain mandatory.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Treating neural depth network outputs as calibrated geometric covariances without empirical residual validation.*

Monocular depth estimation backbones and bird's-eye-view (BEV) lifting transformers output continuous depth fields or discrete depth-bin categorical distributions. Engineers often mistake these softmax spreads or secondary network confidence heads for calibrated geometric uncertainties ($\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$), passing them directly into extended Kalman filters (@sec-perception-state-estimation) or control barrier functions (@sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission). In practice, raw neural confidence scores correlate poorly with true physical error distributions. When presented with unfamiliar textures, specular reflections, or occluding object silhouettes, depth networks produce gross multimodal outliers that deviate by tens of standard deviations from physical ground truth. Downstream clearance insets ($C_{\text{inset}}$) must never rely on raw neural variance. Safe execution requires empirical validation against heavy-tailed residual distributions and hard spatial bounds cross-verified by active ranging sensors such as LiDAR or radar.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Relying exclusively on line-of-sight optical sensing for manipulation without tactile contact feedback.*

During reaches and grasps, the robot's own end-effector structures—fingers, palm, and wrist—inevitably occlude the contact interface. Optical cameras cannot observe local normal forces, shear stress distributions, or incipient micro-slip at the boundary between the gripper and the object. Relying exclusively on high-resolution visual perception to ensure grasp stability leads to dropped objects from undetected slipping or crushed workpieces from excessive actuator torque. Tasks that involve physical interaction and delicate object handling require direct contact feedback. Elastomeric tactile sensors and optical skin arrays can track surface shear and incipient micro-slip, while other applications may rely on wrist force-torque transducers, compliant passive mechanics, or fixtured tooling. Sensor selection must reflect the physical contact dynamics of the manipulation task rather than defaulting to line-of-sight optical cameras.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Assuming active LiDAR and depth sensors are immune to specular reflections and multipath interference in built environments.*

A common misconception is that active time-of-flight LiDAR and depth sensors are immune to optical artifacts because they project their own structured energy. In industrial facilities and built environments, surfaces routinely violate the diffuse Lambertian scattering assumption. Polished concrete floors, metallic shelving, architectural glass partitions, and shrink-wrapped pallet freight cause severe specular reflection. Emitted laser pulses deflect away from the receiver at shallow incidence angles, causing complete signal loss and creating artificial dropouts ("puddle black holes") on polished or wet floors. Conversely, multi-bounce reflections bounce pulses across multiple reflective surfaces before returning to the detector, generating phantom obstacles that appear meters behind solid walls or beneath the floor plane. The observation pipeline must validate return intensity distributions and cross-corroborate surface geometry against complementary inertial and radar channels.

:::
## Summary {#sec-perception-summary}

A perception measurement is actionable only when its capture epoch, clock synchronization bound, coordinate frame, and spatial uncertainty match the kinematic requirements of the intended motion. Sensor selection begins with the physical quantity demanded by the control decision—whether that is photometric appearance, metric range, Doppler radial velocity, or surface contact deformation. Physical capture constraints then determine the exact temporal and geometric validity of that measurement. For rolling-shutter cameras, row-by-row readout creates geometric distortion that must be compensated before triangulation, while an optical bearing ray provides directional bearing but no distance until stereo disparity or active time-of-flight ranging resolves depth. Furthermore, calibration matrices remain valid only within the physical and environmental envelopes under which they were characterized. Latency between exposure and downstream dispatch directly consumes the vehicle's stopping budget. Because an embodied system continues to travel while sensor data moves through serialization, transport, neural inference, and planner admission, unmeasured pipeline delays erode physical clearance margins just as severely as spatial measurement error.

Spatial error deducts from that same physical clearance budget. Stereo depth uncertainty scales quadratically with distance under fixed disparity noise, while angular extrinsic misalignment introduces lever-arm errors that widen linearly with range. System designers cannot rely on nominal datasheets or raw model outputs to establish safety bounds. Zero-mean covariance matrices frequently ignore systematic calibration biases, and classification confidences or learned depth logits do not represent calibrated tail probabilities. Establishing a rigorous 99th-percentile clearance inset requires empirical residual quantiles evaluated directly against ground-truth measurements across the operational domain. Perception delivers individual dated, localized, and qualified measurements; integrating these discrete observations into a coherent state estimate that remains reliable between sensor arrivals is the responsibility of spatial memory.

Silent failures present the most severe operational hazards in physical systems, precisely because dropped frames or overt hardware faults trigger immediate system alerts, whereas misdated frames, saturated detectors, or hallucinated traversable paths arrive without raising error flags. To guard against corrupted data, the perception pipeline enforces an explicit observation contract. Downstream consumers inspect and validate the capture timestamp, clock synchronization bound, reference frame, calibration identifier, error model, and hardware health flags before reading payload buffers. Even with rigorous contracts, confirming semantic truth requires corroboration across independent, complementary sensing modalities.

Seven relations carry the chapter's quantitative argument, and @tbl-08-key-equations records what each bounds or decides.

| Equation                                                                                           | What it bounds or decides                                                                                                              | Derived                          |
|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------|
| $\Delta \mathbf{x} = \int_{t_0}^{t_0+t_{\text{age}}} \mathbf{v}(t)\,dt$                            | The travel an observation's age costs before any consumer can react; at constant speed, $v\,t_{\text{age}}$ enters the stopping budget | @eq-percep-spatial-displacement  |
| $t_{\text{age}} = \tfrac{1}{2}t_{\text{exp}} + t_{\text{readout}} + \dots + t_{\text{IPC}}$        | The capture-to-dispatch age of serialized stages, and which stage dominates it; overlapping stages need a measured interval instead    | @eq-percep-latency-waterfall     |
| $\Delta x(y) = v\,y\,t_{\text{row}}$                                                               | The along-track shear a rolling shutter records, which must be removed before the estimator spends $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ on it         | @eq-percep-rolling-shutter-skew  |
| $\lvert\delta z\rvert \approx \dfrac{z^2}{f b}\lvert\delta d\rvert$                                | How fast stereo depth error grows with range, and so the range beyond which one standard deviation consumes an allowance               | @eq-percep-stereo-uncertainty    |
| $C_{\text{inset}} = C_{\text{safe}} + \lVert\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\text{spatial}}\rVert_{P_{99}}$ | The clearance a consumer holds so the true obstacle stays outside $C_{\text{safe}}$ except with the measured tail probability          | @eq-percep-clearance-inset       |
| $\Delta p = v\,\delta t + \tfrac{1}{2} a\,(\delta t)^2$                                            | The position error a misdated observation carries silently, the reason a wrong timestamp is worse than a lost frame                    | @eq-percep-kinematic-drift       |
| $k = \lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil$                                                                | Which sorted residual sets a clearance inset with coverage $1-\alpha$, and the fewest residuals that can set one                       | @sec-perception-qualifying-error |

: **Key equations of sensor perception**: The relations that turn a sensor's timing and geometry into travel and spatial error, and set the clearance a consumer holds, with the place each is derived. {#tbl-08-key-equations tbl-colwidths="[36,46,18]"}

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Spatial perception and age of information"}
* **Observation Age Begins at Capture and Is Paid in Travel:**\index{Perception!observation age}\index{Perception!blind distance} Hardware-latched exposure timestamps, row readout schedules, and bounded clock conversion enable downstream consumers to compute an exact upper age bound. Every microsecond elapsed from photon arrival to actuator response translates directly into unobserved travel ($d_{\text{blind}} = v \cdot \tau_{\text{delay}}$) deducted from the physical clearance margin.
* **Choose the Measurement for the Decision:**\index{Perception!multimodal fusion} Photometric appearance, metric range, Doppler radial velocity, high-rate edge transitions, and tactile contact deformation address distinct physical questions. Multi-sensor fusion improves system resilience only when sensor spatial coverage and correlated common-cause failure modes are rigorously qualified.
* **Fix the Geometry Before Interpreting It:**\index{Hardware!rolling shutter}\index{Perception!calibration drift} Rolling-shutter readout shears geometric edges under vehicle motion ($\Delta x = v \cdot y \cdot t_{\text{row}}$), requiring per-row pose compensation prior to spatial triangulation. Mechanical vibration and thermal cycling also induce extrinsic calibration drift. An extrinsic shift of `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.theta_ext_str` rad at `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.z_ext_str` projects to `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.dx_ext_str` laterally—consuming the entire localization allowance $\delta_{\text{loc}}$. Consequently, every calibration record must carry an explicit validity envelope that consumers verify prior to inference.
* **A Wrong Timestamp Is Worse Than a Lost Frame:**\index{Perception!timestamp integrity} A dropped frame is an overt failure that triggering systems can handle gracefully, whereas a plausible but misdated frame silently displaces an obstacle's reconstructed position while reporting deceptively narrow uncertainty. Hardware capture timestamps, clock synchronization error bounds, sequence continuity checks, and age validation must always precede payload interpretation.
* **Claimed Error Must Be Measured:**\index{Machine Learning!geometric uncertainty} Softmax classification confidences and depth-bin logits do not characterize spatial tail risk, and zero-mean covariance matrices fail to capture systematic calibration bias. Bounding collision risk requires empirical residual quantiles evaluated against high-precision ground truth across operational conditions to establish defensible clearance insets.
* **The Record Bounds What a Consumer Can Refuse:**\index{Perception!observation contract}\index{Perception!silent failure}\index{Perception!dated snapshots} The observation contract packages capture epoch, clock conversion bounds, reference frame, calibration identity, error bounds, and hardware health flags so the planning permission path can reject untrustworthy claims before reading payload data. Even a fully operational sensor can report a clear path that does not exist, and structured observation tokens do not guarantee that downstream policies compensate for transport latency. Establishing semantic truth requires independent cross-modal verification, and spatial memory must synthesize these dated snapshots into a coherent state that persists through occlusion.
:::

Perception provides the grounded evidence that makes physical action possible—detecting obstacles, identifying surface affordances, and measuring metric range and velocity across complementary sensing modalities. Yet its output remains a sequence of isolated measurements, each strictly bound to a fleeting capture epoch and sensor frame. When an obstacle or human moves behind a barrier, direct perception falls silent. Transforming these discrete historical observations into a durable representation of the physical world—preserving what evidence supports and accounting for what could have changed out of view—is the task of spatial memory and state estimation.
## Historical Perspective and Further Reading {#sec-perception-history}

The geometric foundations of computer vision trace back to photogrammetry and geodesy, where surveyors established rigorous mathematical formulations for optical distortion and perspective projection long before digital processors or mobile robots existed. In the late 1980s, @tsai1987versatile made accurate geometric calibration feasible on off-the-shelf industrial cameras and lenses by developing computationally efficient two-stage optimization algorithms. A decade later, @zhang2000flexible democratized the process by demonstrating that a camera could recover its intrinsic parameters and radial distortion from a planar checkerboard pattern observed at several unconstrained orientations. This formulation transformed camera calibration from an exotic cleanroom procedure into a practical workshop routine. Concurrently, @hartley2003multiple codified the multiple-view projective geometry that underpins stereo disparity, epipolar constraints, and triangulation error. As cameras mounted directly onto robotic manipulators, hand-eye calibration techniques [@shiu1989calibration; @tsai1989new] resolved the rigid kinematic transformations relating camera frames to robot end-effectors. @furgale2013unified generalized this problem to continuous-time systems by integrating temporal delay estimation directly into spatial extrinsics, demonstrating that camera-to-inertial sensor time offsets must be estimated as dynamic parameters rather than assumed to be zero. Together, these developments established an essential systems insight: sensor calibration is never a static constant retrieved from an assembly drawing, but an evolving state estimate bounded by physical drift, mechanical compliance, and thermal expansion.

Sensor hardware diversified along a parallel trajectory as real-time autonomy demanded richer, faster environmental feedback. The autonomous driving competitions of the mid-2000s established scanning laser rangefinders as the primary metric sensor for navigation in unstructured environments [@thrun2006stanley]. Mechanically spinning multi-beam LiDAR systems delivered direct, dense depth measurements, yet their physical rotation introduced significant motion distortion across individual scan lines—a phenomenon requiring per-point timestamping and motion unwinding as detailed in @sec-perception-lidar-age. To overcome the bandwidth and latency limits of synchronous frame-based sensing, neuromorphic engineering [@mead1990] introduced event-based vision sensors featuring independent pixels that emit asynchronous signals only when local log-intensity changes exceed a threshold [@lichtsteiner2008128]. Over the subsequent decade, algorithmic frameworks for event cameras [@gallego2022event] revealed their remarkable microsecond-level temporal resolution and high dynamic range, while also exposing their fundamental limitation: complete blindness to static scenes in the absence of relative motion. Operating high-rate heterogeneous sensors simultaneously required rethinking temporal coordination. Clock synchronization had evolved as a classical problem in distributed computer systems [@lamport1978time], but physical embodiment demanded hardware-level precision. The IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol [@ieee15882002; @ieee15882019] addressed this requirement by embedding hardware timestamping directly into the network physical layer, enabling modern LiDARs, cameras, and compute nodes to align their measurement epochs to a shared master clock that real-time safety monitors can verify.

The third pillar of reliable physical perception is the formal qualification of error. Traditional robotic state estimation frequently assumed Gaussian noise models that systematically underestimated the probability of catastrophic tracking failures in complex environments. Conformal prediction [@vovk2005algorithmic] addressed this vulnerability by proving that exchangeable calibration residuals yield distribution-free prediction regions with exact, non-asymptotic coverage guarantees. @angelopoulos2023gentle made these theoretical foundations accessible to systems practitioners, establishing split-conformal methods as practical tools for safety-critical clearance verification. Modern sensor observation records unite these three technical lineages: each record packages recent calibration revisions, formal network synchronization bounds, and empirical residual distributions. Downstream planning controllers and safety monitors can verify these empirical bounds explicitly rather than placing blind trust in raw transducer outputs.

For further reading, six foundational works elaborate on the geometric modeling, hardware timing, and statistical error qualification developed across this chapter:

- @hartley2003multiple is the classic reference for projective geometry, epipolar constraints, and triangulation, providing the theoretical basis for the stereo depth uncertainty relations analyzed in @sec-perception-error-clearance.
- @szeliski2022computer offers an exhaustive survey of computational image formation, camera calibration, and stereo correspondence from the computer vision perspective, detailing the optical aberrations and sensor transduction phenomena underlying @sec-perception-transduction-calibration.
- @zhang2000flexible presents the ubiquitous planar-pattern calibration method, outlining the closed-form solutions and nonlinear refinement procedures that generate the intrinsic calibration records used throughout production pipelines.
- @furgale2013unified demonstrates continuous-time batch state estimation for multi-sensor suites, proving why temporal offsets between cameras and inertial measurement units must be modeled and optimized as explicit unknowns.
- @gallego2022event provides a thorough review of event-based sensing, tracing hardware architectures from analog pixel circuitry to contemporary tracking and SLAM algorithms while outlining the latency-bandwidth trade-offs relevant to high-speed robotic safety.
- @angelopoulos2023gentle serves as a lucid, practical guide to conformal prediction and distribution-free risk control, clearly articulating the exchangeability conditions that physical distribution shifts—such as floor wear, rain, or abrupt lighting changes—can compromise in real-world deployment.
## Problems {#sec-perception-problems}

```{python}
#| label: perception-problems
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ END-OF-CHAPTER PROBLEM GIVENS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-perception-problems.
# │ Goal:    Print each problem's givens from the registry and the chapter's
# │          cells, and guard the property each problem depends on, so a
# │          registry change cannot silently turn an intended answer around.
# │ Show:    givens only (answers live in the private instructor solutions):
# │          one-tenth allowance share; batches of 2 to 4; 4 m stereo range;
# │          500 residuals; 10 Hz LiDAR mode; Unitree H1 top speed 3.3 m/s.
# │ How:     Reuses SensorInformationAge, RollingShutterSkew, StereoDepthError,
# │          ExtrinsicErrorBudget, ErrorQualification, LidarAge,
# │          NavObservationRecord, and TemporalBatching; recomputes each
# │          guarded property.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_frequency, fmt_percent, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle
H1 = Embodied.Humanoid.Unitree_H1

class PerceptionProblems:
    """Givens for the Chapter 8 problems, with guards on the answers they imply."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    share = 0.10  # category: illustrative (problem given: share of an allowance one error may spend)
    shadow_acc = 0.97  # category: illustrative (problem given: a claimed shadow accuracy)
    z_stereo = 4.0 * meter  # category: illustrative (problem given: stereo claim range)
    n_resid = 500  # category: illustrative (problem given: residuals collected)
    alpha_strict = 0.001  # category: illustrative (problem given: a stricter tail)
    f_lidar_slow = RM.lidar.scan_rate / 2  # category: datasheet (the OS1's 10 Hz mode)
    v_h1 = H1.max_velocity.to(meter / second)  # category: datasheet (registry: Unitree H1 top speed)
    width = RM.footprint_width  # category: illustrative (base footprint width)
    wrist = RM.wrist_camera  # category: datasheet (registry: Sony IMX296, global shutter)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity.to(meter / second)
    t_frame = (1 / RM.nav_camera.frame_rate).to(millisecond)
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond)
    thr = NavObservationRecord.refuse_threshold
    age_2 = (t_age + t_frame).to(millisecond)  # P1: batches of 2, 3, 4
    age_3 = (t_age + 2 * t_frame).to(millisecond)
    age_4 = (t_age + 3 * t_frame).to(millisecond)
    cut_needed = (age_2 - thr).to(millisecond)  # P1: backbone cut for a pair to pass
    budget = (share * AISLE.delta_loc).to(ureg.millimeter)
    t_readout_max = (budget / v).to(millisecond)  # P2
    v_max_rs = (budget / RM.nav_camera.readout_time).to(meter / second)  # P2
    theta_max = (budget / AISLE.d_clear).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude  # P3, rad
    b_needed = (z_stereo**2 * StereoDepthError.sigma_d_px / (StereoDepthError.f_px * budget)).to(meter)  # P4
    n_min_strict = math.ceil((1 - alpha_strict) / alpha_strict)  # P5
    k_500 = math.ceil((n_resid + 1) * (1 - ErrorQualification.alpha))
    t_sync_max = (share * NavObservationRecord.eps_sync / (ErrorQualification.drift_ppm * 1e-6)).to(second)  # P5
    t_sweep_slow = (1 / f_lidar_slow).to(millisecond)  # P6
    age_stream_slow = (t_sweep_slow * LidarAge.sector_deg / 360 + LidarAge.t_data + LidarAge.eps_ptp).to(millisecond)
    age_full_slow = (t_sweep_slow + LidarAge.t_data + LidarAge.eps_ptp).to(millisecond)
    dx_h1 = (v_h1 * t_age).to(ureg.millimeter)  # P7
    skew_h1 = (v_h1 * RM.nav_camera.readout_time).to(ureg.millimeter)
    t_age_h1 = (SensorInformationAge.row_age / v_h1).to(millisecond)
    sensor_side = (RM.nav_camera.exposure_time / 2 + RM.nav_camera.readout_time).to(millisecond)
    wrist_side = (wrist.exposure_time / 2 + wrist.readout_time).to(millisecond)  # P8

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(min(age_2, age_3, age_4) > thr, "P1: every batch of two or more must fail the dispatch-local threshold.")
    check(cut_needed < AISLE.t_backbone, "P1: the pair must be rescuable only by cutting most of the backbone stage.")
    check(t_readout_max < RM.nav_camera.readout_time / 4, "P2: the navigation camera must miss the readout target by more than 4x.")
    check(
        theta_max < math.radians(0.5) and theta_max < LidarSweep.dtheta_sweep.to(radian).magnitude,
        "P3: the tolerable mount error must be far below one LiDAR sweep's yaw.",
    )
    check(b_needed > width, "P4: the required baseline must exceed the base's width.")
    check(n_min_strict == 999 and k_500 == 496, f"P5: conformal answers drifted: {n_min_strict}, {k_500}.")
    check(abs(t_sync_max.magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"P5: sync interval drifted: {t_sync_max}.")
    check(age_full_slow > t_age and age_stream_slow < t_age, "P6: in the 10 Hz mode only streaming must stay younger than the camera.")
    check(
        skew_h1 > AISLE.delta_loc and t_age_h1 < sensor_side,
        "P7: the humanoid must overrun delta_loc and need an age below the camera's sensor-side age.",
    )
    check(wrist.shutter_type == "global" and wrist_side < sensor_side, "P8: the wrist camera must be global shutter with a shorter sensor-side age.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    share_pct_str = fmt_percent(share, precision=0)
    budget_str = fmt_length(budget, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    z_stereo_str = fmt_length(z_stereo, unit=meter, precision=0)
    n_resid_str = fmt_int(n_resid)
    alpha_strict_pct_str = fmt(alpha_strict * 100, precision=1)
    f_lidar_slow_str = fmt_frequency(f_lidar_slow, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    v_h1_str = fmt_velocity(v_h1, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    width_str = fmt_length(width.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=0)
    wrist_exp_str = fmt_latency(wrist.exposure_time.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    wrist_readout_str = fmt_latency(wrist.readout_time.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    wrist_rate_str = fmt_frequency(wrist.frame_rate, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    sweep_yaw_str = LidarSweep.dtheta_sweep_str
    shadow_acc_pct_str = fmt_percent(shadow_acc, precision=0)
```

Each problem specifies its givens, drawn from the machine card (@tbl-01-machine-card), the worked derivations throughout this chapter, or the MLSysIM simulation registry. Any parameter labeled *illustrative* represents an explicit engineering assumption for the exercise rather than a field measurement. Bracketed tags classify the primary task mode (such as Compute, Design, or Critique), while parenthetical labels state the core systems learning objective being evaluated.

1. **[Compute]** (Capture-to-dispatch age) The navigation camera runs at `{python} TemporalBatching.f_frame_str` and dispatches a single frame `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str` after its exposure midpoint (@tbl-08-latency-budget). An engineering team batches consecutive frames into groups of two, three, and four (illustrative) to amortize kernel launch overhead and raise accelerator throughput. Compute the dispatch age of the oldest frame in each batch configuration, and determine which batch sizes satisfy the `{python} NavObservationRecord.refuse_threshold_str` dispatch-local freshness threshold. How much must the `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_backbone_str` feature-backbone stage shrink before a two-frame batch satisfies this bound, and what does this constraint imply about batching frames that support the safety-critical rack-end claim?
2. **[Compute]** (Rolling shutter) Suppose an uncorrected sensor error may consume at most `{python} PerceptionProblems.share_pct_str` percent of the localization error budget $\delta_{\text{loc}} =$ `{python} RollingShutterSkew.delta_loc_str` (illustrative), yielding an error allocation of `{python} PerceptionProblems.budget_str`. Using @eq-percep-rolling-shutter-skew, determine the longest sensor readout duration that constrains along-track rolling-shutter skew within that allocation at the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.v_str` drive limit, and compare your result with the navigation camera's actual `{python} RollingShutterSkew.t_readout_str` readout time. At the camera's actual readout duration, what maximum drive speed would satisfy the same allocation? Evaluate whether the system architecture should adopt a faster sensor, reduce vehicle drive speed, or perform algorithmic motion de-skewing, and state what state-estimation inputs that correction requires.
3. **[Compute]** (Calibration) Holding to the same `{python} PerceptionProblems.budget_str` error allocation, find the maximum mounting-angle error (expressed in both milliradians and degrees) that keeps the projected lever-arm error of a point at the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.z_upright_str` rack-end range within budget. Compare this tolerance against the `{python} PerceptionProblems.sweep_yaw_str` mrad that the base yaws during a single LiDAR sweep in @sec-perception-transduction-calibration. Explain why motion de-skewing must strictly precede any validation check of the LiDAR's extrinsic calibration parameters.
4. **[Compute]** (Clearance evaluation) Consider the stereo camera baseline and optics defined in \ref{nbk-perception-stereo-range-wall}. What physical baseline length would constrain one standard deviation of depth error at `{python} PerceptionProblems.z_stereo_str` to the `{python} PerceptionProblems.budget_str` error allocation? Compare that required baseline against the mobile base's `{python} PerceptionProblems.width_str` footprint width and against the OS1-64 LiDAR's range precision of `{python} LidarSweep.sigma_r_min_str` to `{python} LidarSweep.sigma_r_max_str`. Determine which sensor modality should support a clearance claim at that distance, and specify what physical and calibration uncertainties must still be quantified before either sensor can establish the safety inset $C_{\text{inset}}$.
5. **[Compute]** (Qualifying error) Using the split-conformal rule established in @sec-perception-qualifying-error, calculate the minimum number of calibration residuals required to guarantee a bound at a `{python} PerceptionProblems.alpha_strict_pct_str` percent tail risk (illustrative). Next, for a validation dataset of `{python} PerceptionProblems.n_resid_str` residuals (illustrative), determine which rank index among the sorted residuals defines the empirical `{python} ErrorQualification.alpha_pct_str` percent error bound. Then compute the longest synchronization interval that keeps the OS1-64's `{python} ErrorQualification.drift_ppm_str` ppm oscillator drift within `{python} PerceptionProblems.share_pct_str` percent of the `{python} NavObservationRecord.eps_sync_str` clock-conversion bound. Finally, distinguish which of these parameters a hardware datasheet can reliably provide and which demand a dedicated empirical measurement campaign.
6. **[Compute]** (Capture-to-dispatch age, LiDAR) The OS1-64 can also operate at `{python} PerceptionProblems.f_lidar_slow_str` (an illustrative mode setting). Recalculate the entries of @tbl-08-lidar-age for this lower scan rate: find the forward-sector duration, along with the preprocessing information age under sector streaming vs. full-sweep buffering. How much downstream compute budget does each readout discipline leave before the LiDAR measurement becomes staler than the camera's `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str` dispatch age? Determine whether this slower scan mode remains acceptable for the safety-critical rack-end check.
7. **[Compute]** (Transfer to a humanoid) Consider mounting the warehouse machine's navigation camera and perception pipeline on a Unitree H1 humanoid robot operating at its registry top speed of `{python} PerceptionProblems.v_h1_str`. Compute the robot's physical displacement during the `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str` dispatch age, as well as the resulting along-track rolling-shutter skew at maximum velocity. What dispatch age would constrain platform displacement to the warehouse machine's baseline `{python} SensorInformationAge.row_age_str`? Can this camera hardware ever achieve that target given that the exposure midpoint and sensor readout alone consume `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_readout_str`? Identify the core kinematic assumption of the wheeled mobile manipulator that the humanoid platform violates, and explain the structural perception design change this violation necessitates.
8. **[Design]** (Observation record) Complete the fields of @tbl-08-observation-record-schema for the robot's wrist-mounted camera, which uses a global-shutter sensor operating at `{python} PerceptionProblems.wrist_rate_str` with an exposure time of `{python} PerceptionProblems.wrist_exp_str` and a readout duration of `{python} PerceptionProblems.wrist_readout_str` (from the system registry). Calculate the sensor-side information age from the optical exposure midpoint to the end of readout, and specify the row-timing convention documented in the record. Identify every schema field whose value is not provided in this chapter, and specify the empirical calibration or benchmarking procedure needed to supply it.
9. **[Design]** (Modality selection) Suppose the mobile manipulator must operate in a loading-dock aisle exposed to direct afternoon sunlight through open bay doors and standing water on polished concrete. To validate the rack-end occupancy claim—which requires reliable metric ranging to obstacles within the `{python} LidarAge.d_clear_str` clear distance—select a primary and an independent corroborating sensor modality from @tbl-08-sensor-modalities. For every candidate modality you reject, cite the specific physical failure mode from @sec-perception-failure-modes that disqualifies it in this environment. For each selected modality, specify the real-time health-bitmask flags that its observation record must assert when environmental degradation occurs.
10. **[Critique]** (Learned depth) An engineering team pipes a monocular depth network's per-pixel predicted uncertainty spread directly into the observation record as the measurement covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ and establishes the safety inset $C_{\text{inset}}$ from it, claiming a `{python} StereoDepthError.c_ray_str` ray clearance plus two predicted standard deviations. Identify what physical and statistical guarantees this design omits. Specify the empirical residual collection campaign required to qualify a valid safety inset under distribution-free conformal guarantees (including ground-truth instrumentation, operational domain coverage, sample sizing from the conformal rule, and factors that destroy exchangeability). Finally, explain what default action the safety permission path must execute until that empirical qualification campaign is complete.
11. **[Critique]** (Metric vs. semantic evidence) A slow semantic scene model classifies a LiDAR return inside the robot's stopping envelope as an optical shadow artifact, prompting the motion planner to delete that point from its spatial occupancy map. The engineering team defends this filtering by noting that the model demonstrates `{python} PerceptionProblems.shadow_acc_pct_str` percent accuracy on shadows across its offline test suite (illustrative). Using the metric veto invariant (\ref{psp-perception-metric-veto-invariant}), draft an architectural review comment rejecting this decision. Specify the rigorous runtime qualification test and safety fail-safe mechanism that would be required before the permission path could ever permit such programmatic point suppression.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From sensory photons to spatial memory"}
Perception pipelines deliver time-stamped, qualified measurements of the physical world, but an obstacle or worker at the rack end does not remain continuously in view across successive observation frames. @Sec-memory addresses this temporal gap by fusing dated measurements into a persistent spatial representation, propagating dynamic state estimates and uncertainty bounds across occlusions, and enforcing explicit validity expiries. When sensor dropout or aging observations exhaust the validated motion margin, spatial memory provides the causal justification that allows the safety permission path to refuse motion claims and stop the machine safely.
:::
